vercel-labs/agent-desktop

Computer use CLI for AI agents

Language: Rust

Stars: 16,803

README

# agent-desktop

Computer use for AI agents: see and operate desktop apps on macOS, Windows, and Linux through the OS accessibility tree.

<p>
  <a href="https://vercel.com/labs#labs-products"><img alt="Vercel Labs Product" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/LABS-PRODUCT-0a0a0a.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=Vercel&labelColor=000000" height="28"></a>
  <a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/agent-desktop"><img alt="npm version: agent-desktop" src="https://img.shields.io/npm/v/agent-desktop.svg?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=000000" height="28"></a>
  <a href="https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/blob/main/LICENSE"><img alt="License: Apache-2.0" src="https://img.shields.io/github/license/vercel-labs/agent-desktop.svg?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=000000" height="28"></a>
  <a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/agent-desktop"><img alt="npm downloads per month: agent-desktop" src="https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/agent-desktop.svg?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=000000&label=npm%20downloads" height="28"></a>
</p>

agent-desktop gives an AI agent computer use without screenshots or pixel matching. It reads the accessibility tree of a desktop app and returns it as JSON, with a ref for every element the agent can act on. The agent clicks or types on a ref, reads the UI again to check the result, and repeats. The loop lives in your agent; agent-desktop has no model inside. It ships as a CLI and a C library.

Snapshots, clipboard reads, screenshots, command output, and debug artifacts can contain private desktop content. Keep them out of public logs and uploads.

## Install

```bash
npm install -g agent-desktop
agent-desktop status                # platform, permissions, supported surfaces
agent-desktop permissions --guide   # macOS: walks you through the Accessibility grant
```

Bun, Yarn and pnpm can install the same package. It includes native binaries and platform helpers for x64 and ARM64.
For direct execution without a JavaScript launcher, download the matching native archive from
[GitHub Releases](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/releases) and keep its helper beside the executable.

On macOS and Linux, Homebrew also works: `brew install agent-desktop`. There is no official Scoop package yet.
The repository no longer maintains a custom Homebrew tap or Scoop bucket.

Release archives and building from source are covered in [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/installation).

## Quick start

```bash
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i      # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-desktop click @s8f3k2p9:e8            # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-desktop snapshot --app Finder -i      # observe again to verify
```

Each command prints one JSON envelope. A trimmed snapshot:

```json
{
  "version": "2.6",
  "ok": true,
  "command": "snapshot",
  "data": {
    "app": "Finder",
    "snapshot_id": "s8f3k2p9",
    "ref_count": 59,
    "complete": true,
    "tree": {
      "role": "window",
      "name": "Downloads",
      "children": [
        { "role": "treeitem", "name": "Documents", "ref_id": "@s8f3k2p9:e8", "available_actions": ["Click"] }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

- **Refs belong to their snapshot.** A bare `@e8` is rejected with `INVALID_ARGS`. When the UI changes, an action
  returns `STALE_REF` or `AMBIGUOUS_TARGET`: take a new snapshot and use its refs.
- **Several windows** give `AMBIGUOUS_TARGET`; `snapshot` lists the candidate window ids in `error.details`. Pass one
  with `--window-id`.
- **Dense apps:** map first with `snapshot --skeleton --app Slack -i --compact`, then drill into one region with
  `snapshot --root @s8f3k2p9:e3 -i --compact`.
- **Headless by default.** Ref actions use the accessibility API without moving the pointer or taking focus. The global
  `--headed` flag allows physical input.
- **Post-action waits** observe the ref's original process. Window-owned refs stay pinned to their original window,
  including refs captured from a sheet, alert, popover, focused view, or Linux menu. macOS application menus keep
  their application-owned surface and need no document window. The wait reads the whole pinned window, so overlay
  selectors share its scope. [Wait scope and results](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/configuration#post-action-wait-flags)
  describe the selector limits.
- `type`, `set-value`, and `clipboard-set` accept `--stdin` for piped text, keeping it out of process arguments. Run secret steps as separate commands; batch JSON text appears in process arguments.
- **PowerShell.** Quote every ref (`'@s8f3k2p9:e8'`), because a bare `@token` is the splatting operator.

The full walkthrough is in the [quick start](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/quick-start).

## How it works

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="assets/architecture-dark.png">
  <img alt="The calling agent runs the agent-desktop CLI or the C library. Both go through agent-desktop-core and the PlatformAdapter trait to one platform crate, chosen at compile time, which reads the target app through the AX API on macOS, UI Automation on Windows, or AT-SPI on Linux." src="assets/architecture-light.png" width="720">
</picture>

Your agent calls the CLI, or the C library in process. Both run the same core, which reaches the OS only through `PlatformAdapter`. Each binary is built for one OS and talks to that OS's accessibility API.

## For AI agents

The binary carries guides that match its version:

```bash
agent-desktop skills get desktop      # the loop, refs, verification and retry rules
agent-desktop skills get platform     # what differs on the OS you run on
agent-desktop <command> --help        # flags for one command
```

Install the skill into an agent harness from [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-desktop/agent-desktop):

```bash
npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop
```

Or add this to your `AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
Use `agent-desktop` to see and operate desktop apps. Before the first use, run
`agent-desktop skills get desktop` and `agent-desktop skills get platform`, and follow them.
```

Retry a failed command only when `error.disposition.retry` is `safe`. See [JSON output](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/json-output) for the envelope, error codes, and exit codes.

### MCP

`agent-desktop mcp` serves every command as an MCP tool over stdio. A tool is named after its command (`desktop_snapshot`, `desktop_click`, `desktop_session_start`), takes that command's arguments, and returns its JSON envelope:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "agent-desktop": { "command": "agent-desktop", "args": ["mcp"] } } }
```

Global flags given to `mcp`, such as `--session`, `--headed` or `--trace`, apply to every call.

## Commands

agent-desktop has 60 command names, 56 operational commands. The other four (`key-down`, `key-up`, `mouse-down`, `mouse-up`) refuse to run until a daemon can release a held key or button. [Commands](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/commands) documents each one.

| Group | Commands |
|---|---|
| Observe | `snapshot`, `find`, `get`, `is`, `screenshot`, `list-surfaces` |
| Act on a ref | `click`, `double-click`, `triple-click`, `right-click`, `type`, `set-value`, `clear`, `focus`, `select`, `toggle`, `check`, `uncheck`, `expand`, `collapse`, `scroll`, `scroll-to` |
| Keyboard and mouse | `press`, `hover`, `drag`, `mouse-move`, `mouse-click`, `mouse-wheel`, `key-down`, `key-up`, `mouse-down`, `mouse-up` |
| Apps and windows | `launch`, `close-app`, `list-apps`, `list-windows`, `list-displays`, `focus-window`, `resize-window`, `move-window`, `minimize`, `maximize`, `restore`, `open-system-surface` |
| Notifications | `list-notifications`, `dismiss-notification`, `dismiss-all-notifications`, `notification-action` |
| Clipboard | `clipboard-get`, `clipboard-set`, `clipboard-clear` |
| Wait | `wait` |
| Sessions | `session`, `trace`, `cursor-overlay` |
| System | `status`, `permissions`, `version`, `batch`, `skills` |

## Platform support

| Platform | Requirement | Accessibility API |
|---|---|---|
| [macOS](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/platforms/macos) | macOS 13 or later, Intel or Apple Silicon | AX API |
| [Windows](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/platforms/windows) | Windows 10 1809 or later, x64 or ARM64 | UI Automation |
| [Linux](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/platforms/linux) | Ubuntu 24.04 or later, x86_64 or aarch64, X11 or Wayland | AT-SPI |

Each platform page lists what works headless, what needs `--headed`, and what refuses.

## C library

Each release ships `libagent_desktop_ffi`, so a program can call agent-desktop in process. See the [C library docs](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/ffi).

```python
import ctypes
lib = ctypes.CDLL("./lib/libagent_desktop_ffi.dylib")
lib.ad_adapter_create.restype = ctypes.c_void_p
lib.ad_adapter_destroy.argtypes = [ctypes.c_void_p]
assert lib.ad_init(7) == 0  # AD_RESULT_OK when the header's AD_ABI_VERSION_MAJOR matches the library
adapter = lib.ad_adapter_create()
lib.ad_adapter_destroy(adapter)
```

## Development

Each platform adapter builds only on its own OS, so scope cargo to the host's packages. On macOS:

```bash
HOST_PKGS=(-p agent-desktop-core -p agent-desktop-macos -p agent-desktop -p agent-desktop-ffi)
cargo test "${HOST_PKGS[@]}"
cargo clippy "${HOST_PKGS[@]}" --all-targets -- -D warnings
```

On Windows, use `agent-desktop-windows` instead of `agent-desktop-macos`; on Linux, `agent-desktop-linux`. [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) lists every gate.

## Documentation

- [Introduction](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop): what it is and how it works
- [Snapshots and refs](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/snapshots-and-refs)
- [Errors and recovery](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/errors-and-recovery)
- [Skills](https://agent-browser.dev/desktop/skills)
- [CONCEPTS.md](CONCEPTS.md): vocabulary
- [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md), [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), [SUPPORT.md](SUPPORT.md)

It's built with love (there's no slop!). Please let me know any frictions at all; I'm intensely focused on continuing to make Worktrunk excellent, and the biggest help is folks posting problems they perceive.

Worktrunk is a CLI for git worktree management, designed for running AI agents in parallel.

Worktrunk's three core commands make worktrees as easy as branches. Plus, Worktrunk has a bunch of quality-of-life features to simplify working with many parallel changes, including hooks to automate local workflows & copy-on-write build caches.

A quick demo:

![Worktrunk Demo](https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/max-sixty/worktrunk-assets@main/assets/docs/light/wt-core.gif)

> ### 📚 Full documentation at [worktrunk.dev](https://worktrunk.dev) 📚

<!-- ⚠️ AUTO-GENERATED from docs/src/content/docs/worktrunk.md#context-git-worktrees..worktrunk-makes-git-worktrees-as-easy-as-branches — edit source to update -->

## Context: git worktrees

AI agents like Claude Code and Codex can handle longer tasks without
supervision, such that it's possible to manage 5-10+ in parallel. Git's native
worktree feature gives each agent its own working directory, so they don't step
on each other's changes.

But the git worktree UX is clunky. Even a task as small as starting a new
worktree requires typing the branch name three times: `git worktree add -b feat
../repo.feat`, then `cd ../repo.feat`.

## Worktrunk makes git worktrees as easy as branches

Worktrees are addressed by branch name; paths are computed from a configurable template. Commands that take a branch also accept the path of the worktree it is checked out in.

<p class="workflow-stage">Start with the core commands</p>

**Core commands:**

<table class="cmd-compare">
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th>Task</th>
      <th>Worktrunk</th>
      <th>Plain git</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Switch worktrees</td>
      <td data-label="Worktrunk"><code>wt switch feat</code></td>
      <td data-label="Plain git"><code>cd ../repo.feat</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Create + start Claude</td>
      <td data-label="Worktrunk"><code>wt switch -c -x claude feat</code></td>
      <td data-label="Plain git"><pre><code>git worktree add -b feat ../repo.feat && \
cd ../repo.feat && \
claude</code></pre></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Clean up</td>
      <td data-label="Worktrunk"><code>wt remove</code></td>
      <td data-label="Plain git"><pre><code>cd ../repo && \
git worktree remove ../repo.feat && \
git branch -d feat</code></pre></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>List with status</td>
      <td data-label="Worktrunk"><code>wt list</code></td>
      <td data-label="Plain git"><span class="cmd-compare-value"><code>git worktree list</code> (paths only)</span></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p class="workflow-stage">Expand into the more advanced commands as needed</p>

<p class="workflow-heading"><strong>Workflow automation:</strong></p>

- **[Hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/)** — run commands on create, pre-merge, post-merge, etc
- **[LLM commit messages](https://worktrunk.dev/llm-commits/)** — generate commit messages from diffs
- **[Merge workflow](https://worktrunk.dev/merge/)** — squash, rebase, merge, clean up in one command
- **[Interactive picker](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#interactive-picker)** — browse worktrees with streaming CI status and diff, log, PR and comment previews
- **[Share build caches](https://worktrunk.dev/step/#wt-step-copy-ignored)** — ten worktrees get `target/`, `node_modules/`, etc without building or copying them (on APFS, btrfs, and XFS)
- **[`wt list --full`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#full-mode)** — [CI status](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#ci-status) and [AI-generated summaries](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#llm-summaries) per branch
- **[PR checkout](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#pull-requests-and-merge-requests)** — `wt switch pr:123` to jump straight to a PR's branch
- **[Dev server per worktree](https://worktrunk.dev/tips-patterns/#dev-server-per-worktree)** — `hash_port` template filter gives each worktree a unique port
- **[Aliases](https://worktrunk.dev/extending/#aliases) & [per-branch variables](https://worktrunk.dev/config/#wt-config-state-vars)** — custom `wt <name>` commands and branch-scoped state for hook templates
- ...and **[lots more](#next-steps)**

Multiple parallel agents, same simple commands:

![Worktrunk omnibus demo: multiple Claude agents in Zellij tabs with hooks, LLM commits, and merge workflow](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/max-sixty/worktrunk-assets/main/assets/docs/light/wt-zellij-omnibus.gif)

<!-- END AUTO-GENERATED -->

<!-- ⚠️ AUTO-GENERATED from docs/src/content/docs/worktrunk.md#install..next-steps — edit source to update -->

## Install

**Homebrew (macOS & Linux):**

```bash
brew install worktrunk && wt config shell install
```

Shell integration allows commands to change directories.

**Cargo:**

```bash
cargo install worktrunk && wt config shell install
```

<details>
<summary><strong>Windows & other</strong></summary>

**Windows.** `wt` defaults to Windows Terminal's command, so Winget additionally installs Worktrunk as `git-wt` to avoid the conflict:

```bash
winget install max-sixty.worktrunk
git-wt config shell install
```

Alternatively, disable Windows Terminal's alias (Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases → "Terminal"/"Terminal Preview") to use `wt` directly.

> Free code signing provided by [SignPath.io](https://signpath.io/), certificate by [SignPath Foundation](https://signpath.org/) — [policy](https://worktrunk.dev/code-signing/).

**Arch Linux:**

```bash
sudo pacman -S worktrunk && wt config shell install
```

**Conda / Pixi** (community-maintained [feedstock](https://github.com/conda-forge/worktrunk-feedstock)):

```bash
conda install -c conda-forge worktrunk && wt config shell install
```

Or with [Pixi](https://pixi.sh): `pixi global install worktrunk && wt config shell install`.

</details>

## Quick start

Create a worktree for a new feature:

```console
$ wt switch --create feature-auth
✓ Created branch feature-auth from main and worktree @ ~/repo.feature-auth
```

This creates a new branch and worktree, then switches to it. Do your work, then check all worktrees with [`wt list`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/):

```console
$ wt list
  Branch        Status      HEAD±     main↕    main…±    Remote⇅  Commit    Age  Message
@ feature-auth  +   ↑      +27   -8   ↑1       +31                4bc72dc    2h  Add authenticatio…
^ main              ^⇡                                    ⇡1      0e631ad    1d  Initial commit

○ Showing 2 worktrees, 1 with changes, 1 ahead, hidden: Path
```

The `@` marks the current worktree. `+` means staged changes, `↑1` means 1 commit ahead of main, `⇡` means unpushed commits.

When done, either:

**PR workflow** — commit, push, open a PR, merge via GitHub/GitLab, then clean up:

```bash
wt step commit                    # commit staged changes
gh pr create                      # or glab mr create
wt remove                         # after PR is merged
```

**Local merge** — squash, rebase onto main, fast-forward merge, clean up:

```console
$ wt merge main
◎ Generating commit message and committing changes... (2 files, +53, no squashing needed)
  Add authentication module
✓ Committed changes @ a1b2c3d
◎ Merging 1 commit to main @ a1b2c3d (no rebase needed)
  * a1b2c3d Add authentication module
   auth.rs | 51 +++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
   lib.rs  |  2 ++
   2 files changed, 53 insertions(+)
✓ Merged to main (1 commit, 2 files, +53)
◎ Removing feature-auth worktree & branch in background (same commit as main, _)
○ Switched to worktree for main @ ~/repo
```

For parallel agents, create multiple worktrees and launch an agent in each:

```bash
wt switch -x claude -c feature-a -- 'Add user authentication'
wt switch -x claude -c feature-b -- 'Fix the pagination bug'
wt switch -x claude -c feature-c -- 'Write tests for the API'
```

The `-x` flag runs a command after switching; arguments after `--` are passed to it. Configure [post-start hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/#hook-types) to automate setup (install deps, start dev servers).

## Next steps

- Learn the core commands: [`wt switch`](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/), [`wt list`](https://worktrunk.dev/list/), [`wt merge`](https://worktrunk.dev/merge/), [`wt remove`](https://worktrunk.dev/remove/)
- Set up [hooks](https://worktrunk.dev/hook/) for automated setup
- Explore [LLM commit messages](https://worktrunk.dev/llm-commits/), [interactive
  picker](https://worktrunk.dev/switch/#interactive-picker), [Claude Code integration](https://worktrunk.dev/claude-code/), [CI
  status & PR links](https://worktrunk.dev/list/#ci-status)
- Browse [tips & patterns](https://worktrunk.dev/tips-patterns/) for recipes: aliases, dev servers, databases, agent handoffs, and more
- [Extending Worktrunk](https://worktrunk.dev/extending/) — customize workflows with hooks & aliases
- Watch [@DevOpsToolbox's video on Worktrunk](https://youtu.be/WBQiqr6LevQ?t=345)
- Run `wt --help` or `wt <command> --help` for quick CLI reference

# agent-browser

Browser automation for AI agents: open pages, read them as an accessibility tree, and act on elements from the shell.

<p>
  <a href="https://vercel.com/labs#labs-products"><img alt="Vercel Labs Product" src="https://img.shields.io/badge/LABS-PRODUCT-0a0a0a.svg?style=for-the-badge&logo=Vercel&labelColor=000000" height="28"></a>
  <a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/agent-browser"><img alt="npm version: agent-browser" src="https://img.shields.io/npm/v/agent-browser.svg?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=000000" height="28"></a>
  <a href="https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-browser/blob/main/LICENSE"><img alt="License: Apache-2.0" src="https://img.shields.io/github/license/vercel-labs/agent-browser.svg?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=000000" height="28"></a>
  <a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/agent-browser"><img alt="npm downloads per month: agent-browser" src="https://img.shields.io/npm/dm/agent-browser.svg?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=000000&label=npm%20downloads" height="28"></a>
  <a href="https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-browser"><img alt="skills.sh" src="https://skills.sh/b/vercel-labs/agent-browser?style=for-the-badge" height="28"></a>
</p>

agent-browser is a native Rust CLI that gives an AI agent a browser it can drive one command at a time. `snapshot` returns the page as compact text with a ref such as `@e1` for each element. The agent acts on a ref, reads the page again to check the result, and repeats. The browser stays open between commands, so each step is one short shell call.

## Install

```bash
npm install -g agent-browser
agent-browser install           # download Chrome for Testing (first time only)
```

- **Homebrew:** `brew install agent-browser`, then `agent-browser install`.
- **Linux:** `agent-browser install --with-deps` also installs the browser's system libraries.
- **No install:** `npx agent-browser open example.com`.

Project installs, building from source, `upgrade`, and `doctor` are covered in [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/installation).

## Quick start

```bash
agent-browser open example.com
agent-browser snapshot -i       # interactive elements, each with a ref
agent-browser click @e1         # act on a ref from that snapshot
agent-browser get url           # check the result
agent-browser close
```

The snapshot for `example.com`:

```
- link "Learn more" [ref=e1]
```

- Refs describe the page at the time of the snapshot. After navigation or a DOM change, take a new snapshot before using refs again.
- CSS selectors, text, XPath, and semantic locators also work, for example `agent-browser find role button click --name "Submit"`. See [Selectors](https://agent-browser.dev/selectors).
- A click fails, instead of reporting success, when the target is hidden, disabled, outside the viewport, or covered by another element such as a consent banner. Dismiss the covering element, take a new snapshot, and retry.

The full walkthrough is in the [quick start](https://agent-browser.dev/quick-start).

## How it works

The CLI sends each command to a background daemon that starts on the first command and controls the browser over the Chrome DevTools Protocol. Each `--session` gets its own daemon and browser. By default, the daemon closes a headless browser and exits after one hour without commands, saving state first when [session persistence](https://agent-browser.dev/sessions) is configured.

Chrome for Testing is the default browser. You can also attach to a running Chrome with `--cdp` or `--auto-connect` ([CDP mode](https://agent-browser.dev/cdp-mode)), select the [Lightpanda](https://agent-browser.dev/engines/lightpanda) or [Obscura](https://agent-browser.dev/engines/obscura) engine with `--engine`, drive Mobile Safari in the [iOS Simulator](https://agent-browser.dev/ios), or use a cloud browser provider such as [Browserbase](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browserbase), [Browserless](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browserless), [Browser Use](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/browser-use), [Kernel](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/kernel), or [AgentCore](https://agent-browser.dev/providers/agentcore).

## For AI agents

The CLI ships skills that match its version:

```bash
agent-browser skills get core                 # the core loop, refs, waiting, and common workflows
agent-browser skills get core --ref commands  # one reference, such as the full command list
agent-browser skills get core --full          # adds the full command reference and templates
agent-browser skills list                     # specialized skills: electron, slack, dogfood, and more
```

Install the discovery skill into an agent harness from [skills.sh](https://skills.sh/vercel-labs/agent-browser):

```bash
npx skills add vercel-labs/agent-browser
```

The installed skill is a thin stub that tells the agent to load `agent-browser skills get core`, so its instructions always match the installed CLI. Or add this to your `AGENTS.md`:

```markdown
Use `agent-browser` for browser automation. Before the first use, run
`agent-browser skills get core` and follow it.
```

For MCP clients, `agent-browser mcp` starts an MCP server over stdio. See [MCP server](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#mcp-server).

## Commands

Run `agent-browser --help` for the full list, or `agent-browser <command> --help` for one command.

| Group | Commands | Docs |
|---|---|---|
| Navigate and read | `open`, `back`, `forward`, `reload`, `read`, `snapshot`, `get`, `is` | [Core](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#core), [Snapshots](https://agent-browser.dev/snapshots) |
| Interact | `click`, `dblclick`, `fill`, `type`, `press`, `keyboard`, `hover`, `focus`, `select`, `check`, `uncheck`, `scroll`, `drag`, `upload`, `mouse`, `find` | [Core](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#core), [Find elements](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#find-elements) |
| Wait | `wait` | [Wait](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#wait) |
| Capture | `screenshot`, `pdf`, `record`, `download`, `diff` | [Recording](https://agent-browser.dev/recording), [Diffing](https://agent-browser.dev/diffing), [Files](https://agent-browser.dev/files) |
| Page and network state | `cookies`, `storage`, `network`, `set`, `clipboard`, `eval`, `pushstate` | [Network](https://agent-browser.dev/network), [Settings](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#settings) |
| Tabs, frames, and dialogs | `tab`, `frame`, `dialog` | [Tabs and frames](https://agent-browser.dev/commands#tabs-frames) |
| Debug and performance | `console`, `errors`, `highlight`, `inspect`, `trace`, `profiler`, `vitals`, `react`, `a11y` | [Debugging](https://agent-browser.dev/debugging), [Profiler](https://agent-browser.dev/profiler), [React](https://agent-browser.dev/react) |
| Sessions and auth | `session`, `state`, `auth`, `profiles`, `confirm`, `deny` | [Sessions](https://agent-browser.dev/sessions), [Security](https://agent-browser.dev/security) |
| Agents and integrations | `skills`, `mcp`, `webmcp`, `flow`, `chat`, `batch`, `plugin` | [Skills](https://agent-browser.dev/skills), [WebMCP](https://agent-browser.dev/webmcp), [Plugins](https://agent-browser.dev/plugins) |
| Observe | `stream`, `dashboard` | [Streaming](https://agent-browser.dev/streaming), [Dashboard](https://agent-browser.dev/dashboard) |
| Setup | `install`, `upgrade`, `doctor`, `connect`, `close` | [Installation](https://agent-browser.dev/installation) |

Flags, environment variables, and `agent-browser.json` are documented in [Configuration](https://agent-browser.dev/configuration).

## Platforms

Native binaries ship for macOS (ARM64, x64), Linux (ARM64, x64, glibc and musl), and Windows (x64). The npm package picks the right binary for the host.

## Development

Building from source requires Node.js 24 or later, pnpm 11 or later, and Rust:

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm build:source               # builds the dashboard and the native CLI
pnpm link --global
agent-browser install
```

Run the Rust checks from `cli/`:

```bash
cargo fmt -- --check
cargo clippy
cargo test
cargo test e2e -- --ignored --test-threads=1   # launches real headless Chrome
```

[AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) lists the files to update with each change, the docs checks, and the release process.

## Documentation

- [agent-browser.dev](https://agent-browser.dev): introduction, guides, and reference
- [Commands](https://agent-browser.dev/commands) and [Configuration](https://agent-browser.dev/configuration)
- [Security](https://agent-browser.dev/security): the auth vault, domain allowlists, action policies, and content boundaries
- [Next.js and Vercel](https://agent-browser.dev/next) and [eve](https://agent-browser.dev/eve): running agent-browser in Vercel Sandbox and eve agents
- [Changelog](CHANGELOG.md)

ZapFast is a WhatsApp client written in Rust with
[egui](https://www.egui.rs) and [fastframe](https://fastframe.dev), the
framework behind a family of native desktop apps. It links to your phone as a
companion device through
[whatsapp-rust](https://github.com/oxidezap/whatsapp-rust) and has no browser
engine. In our Linux test it opens in under a second and uses about 200 MB of
idle RAM, against 1.13 GB for WhatsApp Web.
[See the measurements](https://zapfast.rocks/benchmarks/).

The interface is available in English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional),
French, German, Indonesian, Italian, Portuguese (Brazil), Russian, Spanish,
and Turkish.

## Your chats, on your desktop

| Feature | What you can do |
|---|---|
| **Messages** | Send formatted text, replies, edits, reactions, forwards, pictures, files, stickers, GIFs, polls, and voice messages. |
| **Media in the chat** | Play voice messages, videos, round video messages, GIFs, and animated stickers in place. |
| **Your history** | Keep your chats in an encrypted archive on this computer, fetch older messages from your phone as you scroll, and export locally saved chat history as text or a ZIP with downloaded attachments. |
| **Several numbers** | Link more than one WhatsApp number and switch between them in one window. |
| **Desktop controls** | Use keyboard shortcuts, select and copy text across messages, and stay linked in the tray with notifications. |
| **Themes** | Choose light, dark, system appearance, or custom colours. On Omarchy, follow your desktop theme. |
| **Privacy** | Hide locked chats behind a code, or the whole window behind an app lock. Nothing goes to a server of ours. |

## Install

| Platform | Installation |
|---|---|
| **macOS** | `brew install --cask crmne/tap/zapfast`, or [download the Mac app](https://zapfast.rocks/download/#macos). |
| **Arch Linux** | `yay -S zapfast-bin` |
| **Windows** | Choose your build on the [Download page](https://zapfast.rocks/download/#windows). |
| **Other Linux** | Find Nix, AppImage, and other options on the [Download page](https://zapfast.rocks/download/#linux). |
| **From source** | Follow [Getting started](https://zapfast.rocks/getting-started/) for dependencies and commands. |

## Link your phone

1. Open ZapFast. It shows a QR code.
2. On your phone, open WhatsApp, then **Settings**, **Linked devices**,
   **Link a device**, and scan the code. Or click **Link with phone number**
   and enter the eight-character code on your phone.
3. Your recent chats arrive from the phone. Older messages follow as you
   scroll up.

The link survives restarts, and your phone does not need to stay online to
read what ZapFast has already stored. See
[Getting started](https://zapfast.rocks/getting-started/) for the full
walkthrough and [How it links](https://zapfast.rocks/how-it-links/) for the
details.

extremely fast web remote desktop streaming

Language: Rust

Stars: 1,172

README

# voxl

[![crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/voxl-server.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/voxl-server)

Low-latency desktop streaming for the browser, written in Rust. voxl streams an X11
display, a Mac's screen or a Windows desktop as H.264 over a WebSocket to a small web
client that decodes with WebCodecs, with input, clipboard, audio, microphone, file and
folder transfer and dynamic resolution.

## Quick start

```sh
cargo install voxl-server   # needs x264, libyuv, Opus, PulseAudio and esbuild (see Usage)
DISPLAY=:1 voxl             # streams display :1 and prints a link that signs you in
```

Open the link it prints. On a Mac or a Windows PC, `voxl` streams that machine's own
screen instead; see [macOS](#macos) and [Windows](#windows).

## Benchmarks

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/acdf3f31-64fc-4acf-b5c5-ff173d7100a8

In every test below voxl averages 60 FPS with a median latency of 12–99 ms; noVNC
averages under 8 FPS.

A 16 vCPU AMD EPYC 9334 VM (no GPU), 2560x1600 Xvfb desktop, same workloads, each
stream decoded by a native client that reads a pixel marker drawn into the content.
Cells are FPS (worst second), then latency p50/p99 from the content being drawn to the
frame being decoded. voxl's column is its best run of each test. To reproduce, see
[`bench/`](bench/README.md).

- **selkies:** [selkies](https://github.com/selkies-project/selkies) with picom running.
- **KasmVNC:** 1.4.0 with a 60 FPS cap, JPEG/WebP quality 8–9 and video mode, no
  compositor.
- **Neko:** [m1k1o/neko](https://github.com/m1k1o/neko) 3.2 with its defaults (VP8, 25
  FPS). **Neko, tuned** captures at 60 FPS and encodes with x264 `ultrafast`/
  `zerolatency` at up to 30 Mbps, like voxl. Neither adapts its bitrate (Neko's
  estimator is off by default), so on slow links frames queue up; "stalls" means no
  frame arrived in 20 s.
- **Sunshine:** [Sunshine](https://github.com/LizardByte/Sunshine) 2025.628 streaming to
  Moonlight ([moonlight-embedded](https://github.com/moonlight-stream/moonlight-embedded)
  2.7, patched to hand frames to the benchmark client). Sunshine is built around GPU
  capture and encoding; without a GPU it falls back to copying the X11 screen and x264,
  so these numbers show it on a GPU-less VM like the other tests, not on the gaming PC
  it's made for. **Sunshine** runs its defaults (`superfast` on 2 threads) at Moonlight's
  default 40 Mbps; **Sunshine, tuned** uses `ultrafast` on 4 threads at 30 Mbps, like
  voxl (8 or 16 threads did no better). Neither reaches 60 FPS on this VM, and it keeps
  working while the screen is still (its idle CPU). Moonlight doesn't adapt its bitrate,
  so on slow links it's set to 80% of the link. Its CPU was measured in a later session,
  where voxl used 1.74, 1.65 and 1.99 cores on the same workloads.
- **noVNC:** x11vnc and noVNC as [E2B Desktop](https://github.com/e2b-dev/desktop)
  and Daytona ship them (`-forever -wait 50 -shared`, Tight encoding). x11vnc polls the
  screen, which caps it at 6–8 FPS.
- **Daytona:** a default sandbox (1 CPU, x11vnc and noVNC at 2560x1600) streamed
  through Daytona's signed preview proxy, about 12 ms away, which its latency includes.
  The workloads run inside the sandbox, sharing its CPU, and slow links are added on top
  of that internet path.
- **Links:** a bottleneck with a deep queue: a TCP proxy for the WebSocket servers, and
  `tc netem` for Neko's WebRTC media and Sunshine's video (UDP). None of them drop
  packets, where UDP with error correction would have the edge.

## Usage

Build (needs Rust, pkg-config, clang, x264, libyuv, libopus, libpulse and esbuild;
`nix-shell` provides them all):

```sh
nix-shell
cargo build --release
```

Or install it from [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/voxl-server) with the same
libraries on your system (the crate is `voxl-server`, the binary is `voxl`):

```sh
cargo install voxl-server
```

overlay):

```sh
DISPLAY=:1 ./target/release/voxl --port=6901
# prints: open http://localhost:6901/?token=4f1c… to sign in
```

(`nix-build -E 'with import <nixpkgs> {}; callPackage ./xvfb.nix {}'`) for smooth
scrolling. voxl accepts selkies' command-line flags; other selkies flags are ignored.
`voxl --help` lists every flag with its default, and `voxl --version` prints the version.

| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

| `--title`                                                      | `Voxl Computer Stream`             | the page's title: the browser tab, and the app's name if a viewer installs it                                     |
| `--favicon`                                                    | voxl's icon                        | the tab's icon: an `.ico`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp` or `.svg` file                                                 |
| `--enable-basic-auth`                                          | `true`                             | ask for a password (see [Login](#login)); `false` serves without one                                              |
| `--basic-auth-password`                                        | `VOXL_PASSWORD`, else made up      | the password                                                                                                      |
| `--basic-auth-user`                                            | any                                | the user name a browser's sign-in has to give                                                                     |
| `--framerate`                                                  | `60`                               | max frames per second (`60-60` style ranges accepted)                                                             |
| `--preset`                                                     | `ultrafast`                        | x264 preset                                                                                                       |

| `--min-kbps`                                                   | `2000`                             | adaptive bitrate floor                                                                                            |
| `--paintover-crf`, `--paintover-burst`, `--paintover-delay-ms` | `16`, `3`, `150`                   | sharpening when the screen goes still                                                                             |
| `--enable-clipboard`                                           | `true`                             | `true`, `in`, `out` or `false`                                                                                    |
| `--audio-enabled`, `--audio-device-name`, `--audio-bitrate`    | `true`, `output.monitor`, `128000` | desktop audio                                                                                                     |
| `--enable-resize`, `--resize-scale`                            | `false`, `1.5`                     | desktop follows the viewer's window; desktop pixels per CSS pixel                                                 |
| `--microphone-enabled`, `--microphone-fifo`                    | `false`, `/tmp/voxl-mic.fifo`      | browser microphone into the FIFO a PulseAudio pipe source reads                                                   |

| `--files-root`                                                 | `$HOME`                            | folder the Files panel can see; nothing outside it is reachable                                                   |
| `--upload-dir`                                                 | `Downloads`                        | folder (under the root) the panel opens and uploads into; created on first upload                                 |
| `--max-upload-mb`                                              | `0` (no limit)                     | largest accepted upload                                                                                           |
| `--max-record-seconds`                                         | `300`                              | longest recording (`/record`)                                                                                     |
| `--convert-threads`, `--coalesce-us`                           | `4`, `0`                           | tuning                                                                                                            |

### Login

voxl asks for a password before it shows the desktop or takes input, files or API
calls. Give it one with `--basic-auth-password` or `VOXL_PASSWORD`; otherwise it makes
one up when it starts and prints a link that signs you in. There are three ways in:

- **The link**: `http://host:6901/?token=<password>`. The page passes the password on to
  its own connections, so the link also works as an iframe's `src`.
- **The browser's sign-in prompt**, which voxl's page brings up: any user name (unless
  `--basic-auth-user` names one) and the password. Password managers offer to save it.
- **For programs**: `Authorization: Bearer <password>`, or `curl -u :<password>`.

The page's scripts and `/healthz` load without it. If voxl sits behind a proxy that signs
people in itself, `--enable-basic-auth=false` turns voxl's login off.

### Hosts and origins

voxl only answers requests for an IP address or `localhost`, and only from its own page.
That keeps out other web pages, which browsers let connect to any address, including
pages whose domain is pointed at voxl's address (DNS rebinding). To reach voxl under a
host name, such as through a proxy or as `my-pc.local`, name it with `--allowed-hosts`.
To let a page on another site connect, name that site with `--allowed-origins`.
Programs that aren't browsers (curl, scripts, agents) send no `Origin` and connect as
usual. A refused request gets a 403 that names the flag to add.

### For agents and scripts

Screenshots and recordings (start voxl with `VOXL_PASSWORD` set, and send it along):

```sh
# the screen as a PNG
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" -o shot.png localhost:6901/screenshot
# an MP4 of the next 10 s
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" -o clip.mp4 "localhost:6901/record?seconds=10"
# or start...
id=$(curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" -s -X POST localhost:6901/record/start | jq .id)
# ...and stop when done
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" -o clip.mp4 -X POST "localhost:6901/record/stop?id=$id"
```

A recording is the H.264 voxl already sends to viewers, saved as MP4 without encoding
it again, so it costs no extra CPU. It doesn't include the cursor (viewers draw it), and
a resize ends it.

`/wait` returns when the screen settles or changes, so an agent doesn't have to sleep
after every action and hope it was long enough:

```sh
# once nothing changed for 300 ms
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" localhost:6901/wait
# still for 1 s, giving up after 30 s
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" "localhost:6901/wait?idle=1000&timeout=30000"
# the first change in that rectangle
curl -u ":$VOXL_PASSWORD" "localhost:6901/wait?change&region=0,0,800,600"
# {"changed":true,"timed_out":false,"seq":812,"waited_ms":340}
```

## Dependencies

Desktop versions use Flutter or Sciter (deprecated) for GUI. This tutorial is for Sciter only, since it is easier and more friendly to start. Check out our [CI](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/blob/master/.github/workflows/flutter-build.yml) for building the Flutter version.

Please download Sciter dynamic library yourself.

[Windows](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/c-smile/sciter-sdk/master/bin.win/x64/sciter.dll) |
[Linux](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/c-smile/sciter-sdk/master/bin.lnx/x64/libsciter-gtk.so) |
[macOS](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/c-smile/sciter-sdk/master/bin.osx/libsciter.dylib)

## Raw Steps to build

- Prepare your Rust development env and C++ build env

- Install [vcpkg](https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg), and set `VCPKG_ROOT` env variable correctly

  - Windows: vcpkg install libvpx:x64-windows-static libyuv:x64-windows-static opus:x64-windows-static aom:x64-windows-static
  - Linux/macOS: vcpkg install libvpx libyuv opus aom

- run `cargo run`

## [Build](https://rustdesk.com/docs/en/dev/build/)

## How to Build on Linux

### Ubuntu 18 (Debian 10)

```sh
sudo apt install -y zip g++ gcc git curl wget nasm yasm libgtk-3-dev clang libxcb-randr0-dev libxdo-dev \
        libxfixes-dev libxcb-shape0-dev libxcb-xfixes0-dev libasound2-dev libpulse-dev cmake make \
        libclang-dev ninja-build libgstreamer1.0-dev libgstreamer-plugins-base1.0-dev
```

### openSUSE Tumbleweed

```sh
sudo zypper install gcc-c++ git curl wget nasm yasm gcc gtk3-devel clang libxcb-devel libXfixes-devel cmake alsa-lib-devel gstreamer-devel gstreamer-plugins-base-devel xdotool-devel
```

### Fedora 28 (CentOS 8)

```sh
sudo yum -y install gcc-c++ git curl wget nasm yasm gcc gtk3-devel clang libxcb-devel libxdo-devel libXfixes-devel pulseaudio-libs-devel cmake alsa-lib-devel gstreamer1-devel gstreamer1-plugins-base-devel
```

### Arch (Manjaro)

```sh
sudo pacman -Syu --needed unzip git cmake gcc curl wget yasm nasm zip make pkg-config clang gtk3 xdotool libxcb libxfixes alsa-lib pipewire
```

### Install vcpkg

```sh
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/vcpkg
cd vcpkg
git checkout 2023.04.15
cd ..
vcpkg/bootstrap-vcpkg.sh
export VCPKG_ROOT=$HOME/vcpkg
vcpkg/vcpkg install libvpx libyuv opus aom
```

### Fix libvpx (For Fedora)

```sh
cd vcpkg/buildtrees/libvpx/src
cd *
./configure
sed -i 's/CFLAGS+=-I/CFLAGS+=-fPIC -I/g' Makefile
sed -i 's/CXXFLAGS+=-I/CXXFLAGS+=-fPIC -I/g' Makefile
make
cp libvpx.a $HOME/vcpkg/installed/x64-linux/lib/
cd
```

### Build

```sh
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh
source $HOME/.cargo/env
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk
cd rustdesk
mkdir -p target/debug
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/c-smile/sciter-sdk/master/bin.lnx/x64/libsciter-gtk.so
mv libsciter-gtk.so target/debug
VCPKG_ROOT=$HOME/vcpkg cargo run
```

## How to build with Docker

Begin by cloning the repository and building the Docker container:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk
cd rustdesk
git submodule update --init --recursive
docker build -t "rustdesk-builder" .
```

Then, each time you need to build the application, run the following command:

```sh
docker run --rm -it -v $PWD:/home/user/rustdesk -v rustdesk-git-cache:/home/user/.cargo/git -v rustdesk-registry-cache:/home/user/.cargo/registry -e PUID="$(id -u)" -e PGID="$(id -g)" rustdesk-builder
```

Note that the first build may take longer before dependencies are cached, subsequent builds will be faster. Additionally, if you need to specify different arguments to the build command, you may do so at the end of the command in the `<OPTIONAL-ARGS>` position. For instance, if you wanted to build an optimized release version, you would run the command above followed by `--release`. The resulting executable will be available in the target folder on your system, and can be run with:

```sh
target/debug/rustdesk
```

Or, if you're running a release executable:

```sh
target/release/rustdesk
```

Please ensure that you run these commands from the root of the RustDesk repository, or the application may not find the required resources. Also note that other cargo subcommands such as `install` or `run` are not currently supported via this method as they would install or run the program inside the container instead of the host.

## File Structure

- **[libs/hbb_common](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/libs/hbb_common)**: video codec, config, tcp/udp wrapper, and some other utility functions shared with the server
- **[libs/base](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/libs/base)**: protobuf, fs functions for file transfer, keyboard and platform code used only by this app
- **[libs/scrap](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/libs/scrap)**: screen capture
- **[libs/enigo](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/libs/enigo)**: platform specific keyboard/mouse control
- **[libs/clipboard](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/libs/clipboard)**: file copy and paste implementation for Windows, Linux, macOS.
- **[src/ui](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/src/ui)**: obsolete Sciter UI (deprecated)
- **[src/server](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/src/server)**: audio/clipboard/input/video services, and network connections
- **[src/client.rs](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/src/client.rs)**: start a peer connection
- **[src/rendezvous_mediator.rs](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/src/rendezvous_mediator.rs)**: Communicate with [rustdesk-server](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk-server), wait for remote direct (TCP hole punching) or relayed connection
- **[src/platform](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/src/platform)**: platform specific code
- **[flutter](https://github.com/rustdesk/rustdesk/tree/master/flutter)**: Flutter code for desktop and mobile

longbridge/gpui-kit

Rust GUI components for building fantastic cross-platform desktop application by using GPUI.

Language: Rust

Stars: 19,401

Forks: 1,206

Stars today: 285 stars today

README

<p align="center">
  <img src="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/longbridge/gpui-kit/main/website/public/logo.svg" width="112" alt="GPUI Kit logo" />
  <br>
  <strong>GPUI Kit</strong>
</p>

[English](./README.md) | [简体中文](./README.zh-CN.md)

[![Build Status](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![Docs](https://docs.rs/gpui-kit/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/gpui-kit/) [![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/gpui-kit.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/gpui-kit)

Build fantastic, high-performance desktop apps with Rust and GPUI.

GPUI Kit is a comprehensive Rust desktop application framework. It combines a
production-ready UI system with application-grade data, layout, and editing
capabilities, all built on a reusable foundation of behavior, state, and
infrastructure. GPUI Kit ships 75+ documented components and primitives,
WebAssembly support, AccessKit accessibility, UI integration testing, and an
optional JavaScript extension runtime.

Documentation: <https://gpui-kit.com>

```text
gpui-kit             The one crate applications depend on
├── gpui-base        Unstyled behavior, state, and infrastructure
└── gpui-component   GPUI Component: the complete styled UI system
```

`gpui-kit` pins the matching GPUI release and re-exports GPUI, base, component,
and assets, so a Rust application lists a single dependency. JavaScript extension
hosts add `gpui-shell` separately; its default `components` feature supplies the styled catalog.

See the [executable application recipe and AI-assisted development acceptance checks](examples/ai_recipes/README.md) for a tested starting point and verification commands.

## Features

- **75+ Components and Primitives**: Forms, navigation, overlays, data display, editing, feedback, and layout, with polished interactions and productive defaults.
- **Production Ready**: Used to build Longbridge Pro from day one and continuously refined in a publicly shipped commercial desktop application.
- **WebAssembly**: Run applications and the same component showcases on the web with `wasm32-unknown-unknown`.
- **Accessibility**: AccessKit roles, names, states, relationships, and actions are built into the interaction layer and covered by tests.
- **UI Integration Testing**: Render real components in headless windows, drive pointer and keyboard input, and assert state, focus, layout, and accessibility.
- **Native Feel**: Modern controls inspired by macOS and Windows, backed by semantic themes and multiple sizes.
- **120 FPS**: GPU-accelerated interfaces that remain smooth under load.
- **Data Tables**: Virtual scrolling, fixed and resizable columns, sorting, and cell selection across hundreds of thousands of rows.
- **Virtual Lists**: Render only the visible range, including lists whose items have different sizes.
- **Code Editor**: Stable performance at 200K lines with Tree-sitter highlighting and LSP diagnostics, completion, and hover.
- **Dock Layout**: Resizable panels, draggable tabs, nested splits, and edge docks — all serializable.
- **Rich Content**: Native Markdown and HTML rendering, syntax highlighting, and built-in charts.
- **Design Freedom**: Use the complete visual system or build your own on the behavior and infrastructure in `gpui-base`.
- **JavaScript Extensions**: `gpui-shell` lets a shipped Rust host load panels and business logic as scripts, with every capability granted explicitly.
- **Cross Platform**: Ship one Rust codebase to macOS, Windows, and Linux.

## Framework Architecture

### Three layers. One ecosystem.

Use `gpui-component` to keep the application coherent with one complete visual
and interaction system. Use `gpui-base` when your product needs to create and
own that system itself. Use `gpui-shell` when the application should be
extensible in JavaScript after it ships.

| **`gpui-component`**             | **`gpui-base`**                               | **`gpui-shell`**                           |
| -------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Complete, styled components      | Unstyled behavior and infrastructure          | JavaScript runtime hosted by Rust          |
| Productive defaults with theming | Full control over structure and visual design | Capabilities granted one at a time         |
| Best for building applications   | Best for building design systems              | Best for plugins and scripted applications |

```text
                             APPLICATION
                                  │
              ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
              │                   │                   │
              ▼                   ▼                   ▼
    ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐
    │  gpui-component  │ │ Your Design      │ │    gpui-shell    │
    │    Styled UI     │ │ System           │ │  JS extensions   │
    └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘
             │                    │                    │
             └────────────────────┼────────────────────┘
                                  ▼
                        ┌──────────────────┐
                        │    gpui-base     │
                        │ Behavior · State │
                        │ Infrastructure   │
                        └────────┬─────────┘
                                 ▼
                               GPUI
```

> **Behavior belongs to the foundation. Presentation belongs to the application.**

Use **`gpui-component`** when you want polished controls ready to ship. Build on
**`gpui-base`** when your application should own its component source, layout,
styling, and motion while reusing difficult interaction behavior. Add
**`gpui-shell`** when contributors should extend the product without a fork or
a release.

The layering follows the same separation that makes the
[shadcn](https://ui.shadcn.com) ecosystem flexible:

| GPUI Kit ecosystem                   | Web ecosystem                   |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------- |
| GPUI                                 | HTML + Tailwind CSS             |
| [`gpui-base`](crates/base/README.md) | [Base UI](https://base-ui.com)  |
| `gpui-component`                     | shadcn's styled component layer |

[Explore the architecture →](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md)

## Showcase

GPUI Kit has powered [Longbridge Pro](https://longbridge.com/desktop)
from day one. The framework is extracted from the demands of a publicly shipped
commercial desktop application rather than designed in isolation.

> **GPUI provides the rendering foundation. Longbridge provides the production foundation.**

<img width="1763" alt="Image" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e1ecb9c3-2dd3-431e-bd97-5a819c30e551" />

## Usage

```toml
[dependencies]
gpui-kit = "0.7"
```

`gpui-kit` always brings in GPUI and `gpui-base`; `gpui-component` and the
default icon set are on by default. Turn default
features off to keep only the layers you use. The `gpui-component` features (`inspector`, `decimal`,
`tree-sitter`, and each `tree-sitter-<language>`) are available under the same
names.

### GPUI Fast

Enable the optional `gpui-fast` feature to select [GPUI Fast](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-fast)
for the core, native platforms, WebAssembly, and every enabled Kit layer:

```toml
[dependencies]
gpui-kit = { version = "0.7", features = ["gpui-fast"] }
```

Keep the same imports, initialization, and test macros; no application `[patch]`
or crate alias is needed. The default backend remains the pinned upstream GPUI
snapshot. Cargo features are additive, so upstream packages still compile when
Fast is selected. See [Getting Started](https://gpui-kit.com/docs/getting-started)
for feature combinations and comparison commands.

### Basic Example

```rs
use gpui_kit::component::button::*;
use gpui_kit::component::*;
use gpui_kit::*;

pub struct HelloWorld;
impl Render for HelloWorld {
    fn render(&mut self, _: &mut Window, _: &mut Context<Self>) -> impl IntoElement {
        div()
            .v_flex()
            .gap_2()
            .size_full()
            .items_center()
            .justify_center()
            .child("Hello, World!")
            .child(
                Button::new("ok")
                    .primary()
                    .label("Let's Go!")
                    .on_click(|_, _, _| println!("Clicked!")),
            )
    }
}

fn main() {
    gpui_kit::application().run(move |cx| {
        // This must be called before using any GPUI Component features.
        gpui_kit::init(cx);

        gpui_kit::open_window(WindowOptions::default(), cx, |_, cx| {
            cx.new(|_| HelloWorld)
        })
        .expect("Failed to open window");
    });
}
```

`gpui_kit::open_window` is the application window entry point and always mounts a Base `Root`. Component initialization registers styled window facilities; Cargo features do not select a different root type.

### Icons

The default `assets` feature bundles the [Lucide](https://lucide.dev) icon set
as `gpui-kit-assets`; pass it to the application with
`gpui_kit::application().with_assets(gpui_kit::assets::Assets)`. To ship your
own icons instead, leave that feature out and name the SVG files as defined in
[IconName](https://github.com/longbridge/gpui-kit/blob/main/crates/component/src/icon.rs#L86).

## Skills for AI Coding Agents

Install the GPUI Kit skills for your AI coding agent (Cursor, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex, etc.):

```bash
npx skills add longbridge/gpui-kit
```

| Skill                    | Description                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `gpui-kit`               | Setup, component catalog, usage patterns, GPUI mechanics (elements, entities, async, focus, actions, tests), and the Coding Guides. |
| `gpui-kit-design-guides` | The Design Guides: layout, spacing, hierarchy, interaction states, overlays, and interface copy.                                    |

## Development

### Desktop Gallery (Story)

The `story` crate is a gallery application that showcases all available components. Run it with:

```bash
cargo run
```

### Examples

Some larger examples reuse the `story` gallery components and run as standalone packages:

```bash
# Dock layout system (panels, split views, tabs)
cargo run -p example-dock

# Markdown rendering
cargo run -p example-markdown

# HTML rendering
cargo run -p example-html
```

The `examples` directory also contains standalone examples, each focused on a single feature. Each example is a separate crate, run them with `cargo run -p <name>`:

```bash
# Code editor with LSP support and syntax highlighting
cargo run -p example-editor

# Basic hello world
cargo run -p hello_world

# System monitor (real-time charts with CPU/memory data)
cargo run -p system_monitor

# Window title customization
cargo run -p window_title
```

Check out [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for more details.

## Compare to others

See the [comparison with Iced, egui and Qt 6](https://gpui-kit.com/docs/comparison) on the site.

## Related project: Native Shell

[Native Shell](https://nsh.dev) ([source](https://github.com/longbridge/native-shell)) is a sibling project that lets AI generate UI and renders it natively on iOS, Android, Linux (GTK) and macOS (AppKit). Its GPUI desktop backend is in development and will be built on GPUI Kit.

Existing Apache-2.0 permissions remain; earlier revisions retain their prior terms, and third-party contributions keep their own licenses unless separately authorized. - UI design based on [shadcn/ui](https://ui.shadcn.com), some from [Reui](https://reui.io).
