googleworkspace/cli

Google Workspace CLI — one command-line tool for Drive, Gmail, Calendar, Sheets, Docs, Chat, Admin, and more. Dynamically built from Google Discovery Service. Includes AI agent skills.

Language: Rust

Stars: 32,130

Forks: 1,986

Stars today: 22 stars today

README

<h1 align="center">gws</h1>

**One CLI for all of Google Workspace — built for humans and AI agents.**<br>
Drive, Gmail, Calendar, and every Workspace API. Zero boilerplate. Structured JSON output. 40+ agent skills included.

> [!NOTE]
> This is **not** an officially supported Google product.

<p>
  <a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/@googleworkspace/cli"><img src="https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@googleworkspace/cli" alt="npm version"></a>
  <a href="https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli/blob/main/LICENSE"><img src="https://img.shields.io/github/license/googleworkspace/cli" alt="license"></a>
  <a href="https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli/actions/workflows/ci.yml"><img src="https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/googleworkspace/cli/ci.yml?branch=main&label=CI" alt="CI status"></a>
  <a href="https://www.npmjs.com/package/@googleworkspace/cli"><img src="https://img.shields.io/npm/unpacked-size/@googleworkspace/cli" alt="install size"></a>
</p>
<br>

⬇️ **[Download the latest release for your OS](https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli/releases)**

`gws` doesn't ship a static list of commands. It reads Google's own [Discovery Service](https://developers.google.com/discovery) at runtime and builds its entire command surface dynamically. When Google Workspace adds an API endpoint or method, `gws` picks it up automatically.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> This project is under active development. Expect breaking changes as we march toward v1.0.

## Contents

- [Prerequisites](#prerequisites)
- [Installation](#installation)
- [Quick Start](#quick-start)
- [Why gws?](#why-gws)
- [Authentication](#authentication)
- [AI Agent Skills](#ai-agent-skills)
- [Advanced Usage](#advanced-usage)
- [Environment Variables](#environment-variables)
- [Exit Codes](#exit-codes)
- [Architecture](#architecture)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)
- [Development](#development)

## Prerequisites

- **Node.js 18+** — for `npm install` (or download a pre-built binary from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli/releases))
- **A Google Cloud project** — required for OAuth credentials. You can create one via the [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/) or with the [`gcloud` CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install) or with the `gws auth setup` command.
- **A Google account** with access to Google Workspace

## Installation

The recommended way to install `gws` is to download the pre-built binary for your OS and architecture from the **[GitHub Releases](https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli/releases)** page. Extract the archive and place the `gws` binary in your `$PATH`.

For convenience, you can also use `npm` to automate downloading the appropriate binary from GitHub Releases:

```bash
npm install -g @googleworkspace/cli
```

Or build from source:

```bash
cargo install --git https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli --locked
```

A Nix flake is also available at `github:googleworkspace/cli`

```bash
nix run github:googleworkspace/cli
```

On macOS and Linux, you can also install via [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/):

```bash
brew install googleworkspace-cli
```

## Quick Start

```bash
gws auth setup     # walks you through Google Cloud project config
gws auth login     # subsequent OAuth login
gws drive files list --params '{"pageSize": 5}'
```

## Why gws?

**For humans** — stop writing `curl` calls against REST docs. `gws` gives you `--help` on every resource, `--dry-run` to preview requests, and auto‑pagination.

**For AI agents** — every response is structured JSON. Pair it with the included agent skills and your LLM can manage Workspace without custom tooling.

```bash
# List the 10 most recent files
gws drive files list --params '{"pageSize": 10}'

# Create a spreadsheet
gws sheets spreadsheets create --json '{"properties": {"title": "Q1 Budget"}}'

# Send a Chat message
gws chat spaces messages create \
  --params '{"parent": "spaces/xyz"}' \
  --json '{"text": "Deploy complete."}' \
  --dry-run

# Introspect any method's request/response schema
gws schema drive.files.list

# Stream paginated results as NDJSON
gws drive files list --params '{"pageSize": 100}' --page-all | jq -r '.files[].name'
```

## Authentication

The CLI supports multiple auth workflows so it works on your laptop, in CI, and on a server.

### Which setup should I use?

| I have… | Use |
|---|---|
| `gcloud` installed and authenticated | [`gws auth setup`](#interactive-local-desktop) (fastest) |
| A GCP project but no `gcloud` | [Manual OAuth setup](#manual-oauth-setup-google-cloud-console) |
| An existing OAuth access token | [`GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_TOKEN`](#pre-obtained-access-token) |
| Existing Credentials | [`GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CREDENTIALS_FILE`](#service-account-server-to-server) |

### Interactive (local desktop)

Credentials are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM) with the key stored in your OS keyring (or `~/.config/gws/.encryption_key` when `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_KEYRING_BACKEND=file`).

```bash
gws auth setup       # one-time: creates a Cloud project, enables APIs, logs you in
gws auth login       # subsequent scope selection and login
```

> `gws auth setup` requires the [`gcloud` CLI](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install). If you don't have `gcloud`, use the [manual setup](#manual-oauth-setup-google-cloud-console) below instead.

> [!WARNING]
> **Scope limits in testing mode:** If your OAuth app is unverified (testing mode),
> Google limits consent to ~25 scopes. The `recommended` scope preset includes 85+
> scopes and **will fail** for unverified apps (especially for `@gmail.com` accounts).
> Choose individual services instead to filter the scope picker:
> ```bash
> gws auth login -s drive,gmail,sheets
> ```


### Manual OAuth setup (Google Cloud Console)

Use this when `gws auth setup` cannot automate project/client creation, or when you want explicit control.

1. Open Google Cloud Console in the target project:
   - OAuth consent screen: `https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials/consent?project=<PROJECT_ID>`
   - Credentials: `https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials?project=<PROJECT_ID>`
2. Configure OAuth branding/audience if prompted:
   - App type: **External** (testing mode is fine)
3. Add your account under **Test users**
4. Create an OAuth client:
   - Type: **Desktop app**
5. Download the client JSON and save it to:
   - `~/.config/gws/client_secret.json`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **You must add yourself as a test user.** In the OAuth consent screen, click
> **Test users → Add users** and enter your Google account email. Without this,
> login will fail with a generic "Access blocked" error.

Then run:

```bash
gws auth login
```

### Browser-assisted auth (human or agent)

You can complete OAuth either manually or with browser automation.

- **Human flow**: run `gws auth login`, open the printed URL, approve scopes.
- **Agent-assisted flow**: the agent opens the URL, selects account, handles consent prompts, and returns control once the localhost callback succeeds.

If consent shows **"Google hasn't verified this app"** (testing mode), click **Continue**.
If scope checkboxes appear, select required scopes (or **Select all**) before continuing.

### Headless / CI (export flow)

1. Complete interactive auth on a machine with a browser.
2. Export credentials:
   ```bash
   gws auth export --unmasked > credentials.json
   ```
3. On the headless machine:
   ```bash
   export GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CREDENTIALS_FILE=/path/to/credentials.json
   gws drive files list   # just works
   ```

### Service Account (server-to-server)

Point to your key file; no login needed.

```bash
export GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CREDENTIALS_FILE=/path/to/service-account.json
gws drive files list
```

### Pre-obtained Access Token

Useful when another tool (e.g. `gcloud`) already mints tokens for your environment.

```bash
export GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
```

### Precedence

| Priority | Source                 | Set via                                 |
| -------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| 1        | Access token           | `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_TOKEN`            |
| 2        | Credentials file       | `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CREDENTIALS_FILE` |
| 3        | Encrypted credentials  | `gws auth login`                        |
| 4        | Plaintext credentials  | `~/.config/gws/credentials.json`        |

Environment variables can also live in a `.env` file.

## AI Agent Skills

The repo ships 100+ Agent Skills (`SKILL.md` files) — one for every supported API, plus higher-level helpers for common workflows and 50 curated recipes for Gmail, Drive, Docs, Calendar, and Sheets. See the full [Skills Index](docs/skills.md) for the complete list.

```bash
# Install all skills at once
npx skills add https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli

# Or pick only what you need
npx skills add https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli/tree/main/skills/gws-drive
npx skills add https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli/tree/main/skills/gws-gmail
```

<details>
<summary>OpenClaw setup</summary>

```bash
# Symlink all skills (stays in sync with repo)
ln -s $(pwd)/skills/gws-* ~/.openclaw/skills/

# Or copy specific skills
cp -r skills/gws-drive skills/gws-gmail ~/.openclaw/skills/
```

The `gws-shared` skill includes an `install` block so OpenClaw auto-installs the CLI via `npm` if `gws` isn't on PATH.

</details>

## Gemini CLI Extension

1. Authenticate the CLI first:

   ```bash
   gws auth setup
   ```

2. Install the extension into the Gemini CLI:
   ```bash
   gemini extensions install https://github.com/googleworkspace/cli
   ```

Installing this extension gives your Gemini CLI agent direct access to all `gws` commands and Google Workspace agent skills. Because `gws` handles its own authentication securely, you simply need to authenticate your terminal once prior to using the agent, and the extension will automatically inherit your credentials.

## Advanced Usage

### Multipart Uploads

```bash
gws drive files create --json '{"name": "report.pdf"}' --upload ./report.pdf
```

### Pagination

| Flag                | Description                                    | Default |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `--page-all`        | Auto-paginate, one JSON line per page (NDJSON) | off     |
| `--page-limit <N>`  | Max pages to fetch                             | 10      |
| `--page-delay <MS>` | Delay between pages                            | 100 ms  |

### Google Sheets — Shell Escaping

Sheets ranges use `!` which bash interprets as history expansion. Always wrap values in **single quotes**:

```bash
# Read cells A1:C10 from "Sheet1"
gws sheets spreadsheets values get \
  --params '{"spreadsheetId": "SPREADSHEET_ID", "range": "Sheet1!A1:C10"}'

# Append rows
gws sheets spreadsheets values append \
  --params '{"spreadsheetId": "ID", "range": "Sheet1!A1", "valueInputOption": "USER_ENTERED"}' \
  --json '{"values": [["Name", "Score"], ["Alice", 95]]}'
```

### Helper Commands

Some services ship hand-crafted helper commands alongside the auto-generated Discovery surface. Helper commands are prefixed with `+` so they are visually distinct and never collide with Discovery-generated method names.

Time-aware helpers (`+agenda`, `+standup-report`, `+weekly-digest`, `+meeting-prep`) automatically use your **Google account timezone** (fetched from Calendar Settings API and cached for 24 hours). Override with `--timezone`/`--tz` on `+agenda`, or set the `--timezone` flag for explicit control.

Run `gws <service> --help` to see both Discovery methods and helper commands together.

```bash
gws gmail --help      # shows +send, +reply, +reply-all, +forward, +triage, +watch …
gws calendar --help   # shows +insert, +agenda …
gws drive --help      # shows +upload …
```

**Full helper reference:**

| Service | Command | Description |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `gmail` | `+send` | Send an email |
| `gmail` | `+reply` | Reply to a message (handles threading automatically) |
| `gmail` | `+reply-all` | Reply-all to a message |
| `gmail` | `+forward` | Forward a message to new recipients |
| `gmail` | `+triage` | Show unread inbox summary (sender, subject, date) |
| `gmail` | `+watch` | Watch for new emails and stream them as NDJSON |
| `sheets` | `+append` | Append a row to a spreadsheet |
| `sheets` | `+read` | Read values from a spreadsheet |
| `docs` | `+write` | Append text to a document |
| `chat` | `+send` | Send a message to a space |
| `drive` | `+upload` | Upload a file with automatic metadata |
| `calendar` | `+insert` | Create a new event |
| `calendar` | `+agenda` | Show upcoming events (uses Google account timezone; override with `--timezone`) |
| `script` | `+push` | Replace all files in an Apps Script project with local files |
| `workflow` | `+standup-report` | Today's meetings + open tasks as a standup summary |
| `workflow` | `+meeting-prep` | Prepare for your next meeting: agenda, attendees, and linked docs |
| `workflow` | `+email-to-task` | Convert a Gmail message into a Google Tasks entry |
| `workflow` | `+weekly-digest` | Weekly summary: this week's meetings + unread email count |
| `workflow` | `+file-announce` | Announce a Drive file in a Chat space |
| `events` | `+subscribe` | Subscribe to Workspace events and stream them as NDJSON |
| `events` | `+renew` | Renew/reactivate Workspace Events subscriptions |
| `modelarmor` | `+sanitize-prompt` | Sanitize a user prompt through a Model Armor template |
| `modelarmor` | `+sanitize-response` | Sanitize a model response through a Model Armor template |
| `modelarmor` | `+create-template` | Create a new Model Armor template |

**Examples:**

```bash
# Send an email
gws gmail +send --to alice@example.com --subject "Hello" --body "Hi there"

# Reply to a message
gws gmail +reply --message-id MESSAGE_ID --body "Thanks!"

# Append a row to a spreadsheet
gws sheets +append --spreadsheet SPREADSHEET_ID --values "Alice,95"

# Show today's calendar agenda
gws calendar +agenda

# Upload a file to Drive
gws drive +upload ./report.pdf --name "Q1 Report"

# Morning standup summary
gws workflow +standup-report

# Show today's agenda in a specific timezone
gws calendar +agenda --today --timezone America/New_York
```

### Model Armor (Response Sanitization)

Integrate [Google Cloud Model Armor](https://cloud.google.com/security/products/model-armor) to scan API responses for prompt injection before they reach your agent.

```bash
gws gmail users messages get --params '...' \
  --sanitize "projects/P/locations/L/templates/T"
```

| Variable                                 | Description                  |
| ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_SANITIZE_TEMPLATE` | Default Model Armor template |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_SANITIZE_MODE`     | `warn` (default) or `block`  |

## Environment Variables

All variables are optional. See [`.env.example`](.env.example) for a copy-paste template.

| Variable | Description |
|---|---|
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_TOKEN` | Pre-obtained OAuth2 access token (highest priority) |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CREDENTIALS_FILE` | Path to OAuth credentials JSON (user or service account) |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CLIENT_ID` | OAuth client ID (alternative to `client_secret.json`) |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CLIENT_SECRET` | OAuth client secret (paired with `CLIENT_ID`) |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_CONFIG_DIR` | Override config directory (default: `~/.config/gws`) |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_SANITIZE_TEMPLATE` | Default Model Armor template |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_SANITIZE_MODE` | `warn` (default) or `block` |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_LOG` | Log level for stderr (e.g., `gws=debug`). Off by default. |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_CLI_LOG_FILE` | Directory for JSON log files with daily rotation. Off by default. |
| `GOOGLE_WORKSPACE_PROJECT_ID` | GCP project ID override for quota/billing and fallback for helper commands |

Environment variables can also be set in a `.env` file (loaded via [dotenvy](https://crates.io/crates/dotenvy)).

## Exit Codes

`gws` uses structured exit codes so scripts can branch on the failure type without parsing error output.

| Code | Meaning | Example cause |
|------|---------|---------------|
| `0` | Success | Command completed normally |
| `1` | API error | Google returned a 4xx/5xx response |
| `2` | Auth error | Credentials missing, expired, or invalid |
| `3` | Validation error | Bad arguments, unknown service, invalid flag |
| `4` | Discovery error | Could not fetch the API schema document |
| `5` | Internal error | Unexpected failure |

```bash
gws drive files list --params '{"fileId": "bad"}'
echo $?   # 1 — API error

gws unknown-service files list
echo $?   # 3 — validation error (unknown service)
```

## Architecture

`gws` uses a **two-phase parsing** strategy:

1. Read `argv[1]` to identify the service (e.g. `drive`)
2. Fetch the service's Discovery Document (cached 24 h)
3. Build a `clap::Command` tree from the document's resources and methods
4. Re-parse the remaining arguments
5. Authenticate, build the HTTP request, execute

All output — success, errors, download metadata — is structured JSON.

## Troubleshooting

### "Access blocked" or 403 during login

Your OAuth app is in **testing mode** and your account is not listed as a test user.

**Fix:** Open the [OAuth consent screen](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials/consent) in your GCP project → **Test users** → **Add users** → enter your Google account email. Then retry `gws auth login`.

### "Google hasn't verified this app"

Expected when your app is in testing mode. Click **Advanced** → **Go to \<app name\> (unsafe)** to proceed. This is safe for personal use; verification is only required to publish the app to other users.

### Too many scopes / consent screen error

Unverified (testing mode) apps are limited to ~25 OAuth scopes. The `recommended` scope preset includes many scopes and will exceed this limit.

**Fix:** Select only the scopes you need:

```bash
gws auth login --scopes drive,gmail,calendar
```

### `gcloud` CLI not found

`gws auth setup` requires the `gcloud` CLI to automate project creation. You have three options:

1. [Install gcloud](https://cloud.google.com/sdk/docs/install) and use `gcloud` directly.
2. Re-run `gws auth setup` which wraps `gcloud` calls.
3. Skip `gcloud` entirely — set up OAuth credentials manually in the [Cloud Console](#manual-oauth-setup-google-cloud-console)

### `redirect_uri_mismatch`

The OAuth client was not created as a **Desktop app** type. In the [Credentials](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials) page, delete the existing client, create a new one with type **Desktop app**, and download the new JSON.

### API not enabled — `accessNotConfigured`

If a required Google API is not enabled for your GCP project, you will see a
403 error with reason `accessNotConfigured`:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": 403,
    "message": "Gmail API has not been used in project 549352339482 ...",
    "reason": "accessNotConfigured",
    "enable_url": "https://console.developers.google.com/apis/api/gmail.googleapis.com/overview?project=549352339482"
  }
}
```

`gws` also prints an actionable hint to **stderr**:

```
💡 API not enabled for your GCP project.
   Enable it at: https://console.developers.google.com/apis/api/gmail.googleapis.com/overview?project=549352339482
   After enabling, wait a few seconds and retry your command.
```

**Steps to fix:**

1. Click the `enable_url` link (or copy it from the `enable_url` JSON field).
2. In the GCP Console, click **Enable**.
3. Wait ~10 seconds, then retry your `gws` command.

> [!TIP]
> You can also run `gws auth setup` which walks you through enabling all required
> APIs for your project automatically.

cargo build                       # dev build
cargo clippy -- -D warnings       # lint

## What is mise?

mise (pronounced "meez", short for _mise-en-place_) manages a project's dev
tools, environment variables, and tasks from one `mise.toml` that works across
your shell, editor, and CI:

```toml
[tools]
node = "24"
python = "3.14"
rust = "stable"
"cargo:cargo-nextest" = "0.9"
"github:BurntSushi/ripgrep" = "15"
"npm:prettier" = "3"

[env]
NODE_ENV = "development"
_.file = ".env"
_.path = "./node_modules/.bin"

[tasks.build]
description = "Build the application"
run = "npm run build"

[tasks.test]
description = "Run the test suite"
depends = ["build"]
run = "pytest && npm test"
```

- Install [dev tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/) such as Node.js, Python,
  Go, Rust, and Terraform from a
  [registry of 1,000+ tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/registry.html) or directly
  from [backends](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/backends/) like GitHub
  releases, Aqua, Cargo, npm, and PyPI, with separate versions per project.
- Load [environment variables](https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/), `.env`
  files, `PATH` entries, virtualenvs, and
  [secrets](https://mise.jdx.dev/environments/secrets/) automatically as you
  enter a directory.
- Run [tasks](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/) defined in `mise.toml` or as scripts
  in `mise-tasks/`, with dependencies, parallel execution, file watching, and
  the project's tools and environment already configured.
- Set up a machine with [`mise bootstrap`](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html)
  and [`mise dot apply`](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) to apply system
  packages, dotfiles, Git repositories, macOS defaults, and background services.

Adopt only the parts you need. Start with a single tool or task, and keep any
existing `.tool-versions` files as they are; mise also reads `.nvmrc`,
`.python-version`, and other
[idiomatic version files](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/versions.html#idiomatic-version-files)
once enabled.

[![Demo of mise managing tools](./docs/tapes/demo.gif)](https://mise.jdx.dev/demo.html)

See the [demo transcript](https://mise.jdx.dev/demo.html#transcript) for the
commands shown above.

## Quickstart

### 1. Install mise

On macOS or Linux:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://mise.run | sh
~/.local/bin/mise --version
```

On Windows, run `winget install jdx.mise`. For Homebrew, apt, dnf, Scoop, and
other package managers, see
[Installing mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/installing-mise.html).

The installer places the binary at `~/.local/bin/mise`. If `~/.local/bin` is not
on your `PATH` yet, run `~/.local/bin/mise` in place of `mise` until you
activate mise in step 4.

### 2. Run a tool without changing your shell

```sh
mise exec node@24 -- node --version
# v24.x.x
```

[`mise exec`](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/exec.html) downloads Node.js 24 if
needed and runs the command after `--` with that version on `PATH`. Your shell
and config files stay untouched.

### 3. Configure a project

Create a project directory, select Node.js 24, set an environment variable, and
add a task:

```sh
mkdir my-project && cd my-project
mise use node@24
mise set NODE_ENV=development
mise tasks add hello -- node -e "console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)"
```

These commands install Node.js 24 and write `mise.toml`:

```toml
[tools]
node = "24"

[env]
NODE_ENV = "development"

[tasks.hello]
run = 'node -e "console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)"'
```

Run the task with [`mise run`](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/run.html):

```sh
mise run hello
# [hello] $ node -e "console.log(process.version, process.env.NODE_ENV)"
# v24.x.x development
```

Commit `mise.toml` so teammates and CI get the same setup when they run
`mise install` or `mise run`. `"24"` requests the latest release in the Node.js
24 series; run `mise lock` to record exact versions and checksums in a
[lockfile](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/mise-lock.html), or
`mise use --global node@24` to set a personal default in
`~/.config/mise/config.toml`.

### 4. Activate mise in your shell (optional)

Shell activation updates `PATH` and project environment variables whenever you
change directories, so you can invoke `node` directly without `mise exec`. If
you installed with `mise.run`, run the command for your shell once, then open a
new terminal:

```sh
# bash
echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate bash)"' >> ~/.bashrc

# zsh
echo 'eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate zsh)"' >> "${ZDOTDIR:-$HOME}/.zshrc"

# fish
mkdir -p ~/.config/fish
echo '~/.local/bin/mise activate fish | source' >> ~/.config/fish/config.fish
```

If a package manager installed mise, use `mise` in place of `~/.local/bin/mise`.
With Homebrew, fish activates mise without this step.

For PowerShell, Nushell, Elvish, Xonsh, and IDE or CI shims, see
[Shell setup](https://mise.jdx.dev/shell-setup.html) and
[Shims](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html).

## Everyday commands

| Command                     | Action                                                            |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `mise use node@24`          | Install a tool and record it in the current project's `mise.toml` |
| `mise use --global node@24` | Install a tool and set it as your global default                  |
| `mise install`              | Install all tools declared in the active config files             |
| `mise exec -- <command>`    | Run a command with the project's tools and environment            |
| `mise run <task>`           | Run a project task with its dependencies, tools, and environment  |
| `mise set KEY=value`        | Set an environment variable in `mise.toml`                        |
| `mise env`                  | Print the resolved environment variables and `PATH` changes       |
| `mise ls --current`         | List the tool versions active in the current directory            |
| `mise outdated`             | List tools with newer releases than the installed version         |
| `mise upgrade`              | Install those newer releases                                      |
| `mise lock`                 | Write exact tool versions and checksums to `mise.lock`            |
| `mise config ls`            | Show the config files loaded for the current directory            |
| `mise doctor`               | Check your mise installation, shell activation, and configuration |

## Set up a machine with mise bootstrap

Beyond project directories, `~/.config/mise/config.toml` can declare the state
of your machine:

```toml
[bootstrap.packages]
"apt:build-essential" = "latest"
"brew:jq" = "latest"

[bootstrap.repos]
"~/src/app" = { url = "https://github.com/you/app.git" }

[dotfiles]
"~/.zshrc" = { mode = "track" }
```

Preview and apply the configuration, or bootstrap a new machine directly from a
Git repository:

```sh
mise bootstrap --dry-run
mise bootstrap
mise bootstrap --adopt you/dotfiles
```

See [Bootstrap](https://mise.jdx.dev/bootstrap.html) and
[Dotfiles](https://mise.jdx.dev/dotfiles.html) for supported package managers,
dotfile tracking and templating, services, and remote SSH targets.

[translations for all supported languages](docs/_reference/translating.md#languages-and-coverage).

adds EQ and visualizers on macOS 14.2 or newer, and visualizers on Windows 11,
including MilkDrop. Windows Soloist playback does not support audible EQ.
The Mac route keeps Soloist at full volume after redirecting its output,
then applies Spotifast’s volume after the visualizers, including mute. Phone
volume changes adjust that output level; Spotify’s indicator returns to 100%.
Windows visuals keep their level as Soloist’s volume falls and stop only when it is muted.
When enabled, Soloist appears as **This computer**; settings show the controls
that apply to it. Turning it off restores the built-in player's preferences.
While Soloist starts and its account is verified, the Spotify loading screen shows
**Verifying Soloist…** and waits to accept playback commands. Setup takes three
steps, and ends with choosing the named device in Spotify, with the built-in
player available as a quiet alternative below the card. If Soloist stops later,
a banner over the app says so while Spotifast restarts it, and offers **Try
again** if that does not work. **Settings → Spotify Soloist → Spotify access**
connects the separate Spotify session for Made for you, listening activity and
Spotify lyrics without changing players.

## Your music, on your desktop

| Feature | What you can do |
|---|---|
| **Library and search** | Browse playlists, Liked Songs, albums, artists, and podcasts. Discover upcoming albums on artist pages and open their countdown to pre-save. Search the catalogue and edit playlists you own. Copy a song's link, title, or artists from its menu. |
| **Local files** | Play the local files your playlists list from a folder you choose in Settings, at any sample rate. Names show spaces and accents correctly, including in cached playlists. |
| **Lyrics** | Spotify lyrics when the playback session is signed in, with LRCLIB as fallback. Temporary LRCLIB overloads retry and try search; older cached lyrics remain available during outages. |
| **Spotify Connect** | Play on this computer or control playback on your other devices, including Google Cast speakers and groups. Cast devices appear as they are discovered; frequently and recently chosen outputs rise to the top. Remote volume keeps your chosen level while Spotify updates. |
| **Queue** | Add songs to the queue, or choose **Play next** to put a song or selection first when playing on this computer. |
| **Themes** | Choose light, dark, system appearance, or custom colours, with one theme for light mode and one for dark mode that switch with the system. On Omarchy, follow your desktop theme. |
| **Desktop controls** | Use keyboard shortcuts and media keys. Keep music playing from the tray when supported by your desktop and settings, and start Spotifast with your computer, with its window or in the tray. |
| **Winamp mini player** | Use classic skins with an equalizer, playlist, and animated sound displays. |
| **MilkDrop** | Watch music-reactive visuals in a separate window or full screen. See platform availability below. |

## Install

| Platform | Installation |
|---|---|
| **macOS** | `brew install --cask crmne/tap/spotifast`, or [download the Mac app](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#macos). |
| **Arch Linux** | `yay -S spotifast-bin` |
| **Windows** | The installer or a portable ZIP, for x64 and ARM, from the [Download page](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#windows). |
| **Debian, Ubuntu** | The [DEB package](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#debian-and-ubuntu), then `sudo apt install ./spotifast_*.deb` |
| **Fedora** | The [RPM package](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#fedora), then `sudo dnf install ./spotifast-*.rpm` |
| **Other Linux** | Find Flatpak, AppImage, Nix, and other options on the [Download page](https://spotifast.rocks/download/#linux). |
| **From source** | Follow [Build from source](https://spotifast.rocks/getting-started/#build-from-source) for dependencies and commands. |

## Start listening

1. Register Spotifast with Spotify, as the sign-in screen shows: in the
   [Spotify developer dashboard](https://developer.spotify.com/dashboard),
   click **Create app**, Spotify's name for this registration, with the
   redirect URI `http://127.0.0.1:8989/login` and **Web API** ticked. It takes
   about two minutes and gives you a Client ID. Spotify requires Premium on the
   account that registers, so a Free account can't do this step itself.
   [Getting started](https://spotifast.rocks/getting-started/#make-a-spotify-app)
   has the steps.
2. Paste the Client ID into Spotifast and choose **Sign in with Spotify**.
   Approve access in your browser, then return to the app to see your library.
3. To listen on this computer, open the device menu in the bottom player bar
   and choose **Set up playback here**, also available in Settings.
4. Complete the separate playback approval in your browser. Your computer
   appears as a Spotify Connect device named **Spotifast**.

Library access and local playback have separate approvals. Spotifast remembers
both using your computer's protected storage. See
[Getting started](https://spotifast.rocks/getting-started/) for the full walkthrough
and [How it connects](https://spotifast.rocks/how-it-connects/) for the details.

## The Winamp mini player

A classic look for your music, with Winamp 2 `.wsz` and Windows Media Player `.wmz` skins, an equalizer,
a playlist, and animated sound displays. Switch with **Ctrl+M**
(**Cmd+Shift+M** on macOS), the shrink button, or Settings.
The spectrum analyser and oscilloscope also work in the collapsed title bar.

<p align="center">
  <img src="docs/assets/images/winamp.png" alt="Spotifast's Winamp mini player with the built-in skin, equalizer, and playlist" width="320">
</p>

[Explore the mini player](https://spotifast.rocks/winamp/), including skins,
window sizes, controls, and the return to the main player.

## Music in motion

MilkDrop reacts to music playing on this computer, with more than 10,000
presets downloaded on first use. Open it from the visualiser button,
Settings, or the mini player's **V** menu.

![MilkDrop visualiser displaying coloured concentric patterns in Spotifast](docs/assets/images/milkdrop-poster.jpg)

Included on **Linux**, **macOS**, and **Windows Intel/AMD** builds.
It is not included in the Windows on ARM download.
[Read the MilkDrop guide](https://spotifast.rocks/milkdrop/) for presets,
controls, and fullscreen mode.

## Guides and help

The complete guide lives at **[spotifast.rocks](https://spotifast.rocks/)**.

| You want to… | Read |
|---|---|
| Sign in, set up playback, or configure themes, fonts, and proxies | [Getting started](https://spotifast.rocks/getting-started/) |
| Learn shortcuts, command-line controls, and updates | [Everyday use](https://spotifast.rocks/using-spotifast/) |
| Check storage sizes, clear cached audio and find stored files | [Settings and files](https://spotifast.rocks/settings-and-files/) |
| Understand scrolling performance and reduce loading delays | [Make it even faster](https://spotifast.rocks/make-it-even-faster/) |
| Fix "Spotify refused the audio key" or "Spotify is being slow" | [When something goes wrong](https://spotifast.rocks/troubleshooting/) |
| Understand what is stored and sent | [Privacy](https://spotifast.rocks/privacy/) · [How it connects](https://spotifast.rocks/how-it-connects/) |
| Check Spotify and librespot limitations | [What Spotify allows](https://spotifast.rocks/what-spotify-allows/) |
| Is it safe for my account? | [Account safety](https://spotifast.rocks/what-is-spotifast/#account-safety) |
| Report a bug or propose a feature | Read [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md), then use the [issue forms](https://github.com/crmne/spotifast/issues/new/choose). |

## Contributing

Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before opening an issue or pull
request. To look at the interface without a Spotify account, run:

```sh
cargo run --features demo -- --demo
```

Translations live in `assets/i18n/`; see
[Translating Spotifast](docs/_reference/translating.md). Release packaging
is described in [PACKAGING.md](PACKAGING.md).

## More native apps

**Want WhatsApp just as fast and native?** [ZapFast](https://zapfast.rocks)
is Spotifast's sibling. Both are built on
[fastframe](https://fastframe.dev).

## Spotify Connect updates

With local playback enabled, Spotify pushes changes from other devices over
Spotifast's existing Connect session. Playback changes trigger a refresh.
Volume-only changes appear directly for the active playback device without
an extra request; an unconfirmed volume change made in Spotifast takes
precedence. Push-triggered refreshes are at least a second apart and wait for
a pending playback read to finish. Changes received during that read are
folded into one follow-up.
Connect pushes are ignored when this computer is the active device both
before and after; position-only updates cause no requests. Regular polling
remains the fallback.

## Sonos playback

Sonos speakers use the Spotify Connect session for playback control. Enable
local playback first, then select the speaker in the device picker.

## Acknowledgements

Spotifast uses [librespot](https://github.com/librespot-org/librespot),
[egui](https://www.egui.rs), [fastframe](https://fastframe.dev), the [Inter](https://rsms.me/inter/)
typeface (OFL), and [Lucide](https://lucide.dev) icons (ISC).

Spotifast is an independent project and is not affiliated with Spotify.
Spotify is a trademark of Spotify AB.

## Quickstart

### Installing and running Codex CLI

Run the following on Mac or Linux to install Codex CLI:

```shell
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh
```

Run the following on Windows to install Codex CLI:

```shell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex"
```

The standalone installers download from `https://releases.openai.com/codex` by default and fall back to GitHub Releases if a metadata or asset download is unavailable. To force GitHub Releases, set `CODEX_INSTALLER_USE_RELEASES_OPENAI_COM` to `false` (`0` and `no` are also accepted):

```shell
curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | CODEX_INSTALLER_USE_RELEASES_OPENAI_COM=false sh
```

```powershell
$env:CODEX_INSTALLER_USE_RELEASES_OPENAI_COM='false'; irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex
```

Codex CLI can also be installed via the following package managers:

```shell
# Install using npm
npm install -g @openai/codex
```

```shell
# Install using Homebrew
brew install --cask codex
```

Then simply run `codex` to get started.

<details>
<summary>You can also go to the <a href="https://github.com/openai/codex/releases/latest">latest GitHub Release</a> and download the appropriate binary for your platform.</summary>

Each GitHub Release contains many executables, but in practice, you likely want one of these:

- macOS
  - Apple Silicon/arm64: `codex-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz`
  - x86_64 (older Mac hardware): `codex-x86_64-apple-darwin.tar.gz`
- Linux
  - x86_64: `codex-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz`
  - arm64: `codex-aarch64-unknown-linux-musl.tar.gz`

Each archive contains a single entry with the platform baked into the name (e.g., `codex-x86_64-unknown-linux-musl`), so you likely want to rename it to `codex` after extracting it.

</details>

### Using Codex with your ChatGPT plan

Run `codex` and select **Sign in with ChatGPT**. We recommend signing into your ChatGPT account to use Codex as part of your Plus, Pro, Business, Edu, or Enterprise plan. [Learn more about what's included in your ChatGPT plan](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11369540-codex-in-chatgpt).

You can also use Codex with an API key, but this requires [additional setup](https://developers.openai.com/codex/auth#sign-in-with-an-api-key).

pbakaus/impeccable

The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with polish and bolder, review with critique and audit, catch AI slop before it ships.

Language: Rust

Stars: 103,902

Forks: 6,157

Stars today: 1,280 stars today

README

# Impeccable

The design vocabulary for your coding agent. Steer with `polish` and `bolder`, review with `critique` and `audit`, and catch AI slop before it ships.

From your project root:

```bash
npx impeccable install
```

Reload your coding tool, then run `/impeccable init` in your agent (`$impeccable init` on Codex).

Works with Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Replit Agent, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, Kiro, Trae, Rovo Dev, Qoder, Mistral Vibe, Pi, Hermes Agent, DeepSeek Harness, and Veto. Full docs live at [impeccable.style/docs](https://impeccable.style/docs).

| Without Impeccable | With Impeccable |
|---|---|
| ![Villa Castagneto built without Impeccable: cream background, a thin serif headline with an italic accent, two pill buttons, and flat vector illustrations in rounded cards](https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable/raw/main/docs/images/readme-without.webp) | ![Villa Castagneto built with Impeccable: a full-bleed engraved night scene of the villa on its cliff above the sea, a condensed cream and vermilion headline, and a month strip along the bottom](https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable/raw/main/docs/images/readme-with.webp) |

Same model (Fable 5.1), same brief: a fourteen-room family guesthouse on the Ligurian coast. Without Impeccable, it builds the tasteful default: cream page, thin serif, italic accent, pill buttons. With it, the page is built around one picture: the house at night, seen from the water.

For a full project, see the [Neo Mirai case study](https://impeccable.style/cases/neo-mirai): a conference site taken from mockup to shipped page.

## Why

Inter for everything. Purple-to-blue gradients. Cards nested in cards, gray text on colored backgrounds, a rounded-square icon tile above every heading. Ask an agent for a page with no other guidance and these show up again and again, across models and projects.

- **Words for what you want.** "Make it pop" leaves your agent to guess. `/impeccable bolder the pricing cards` loads a playbook written for that one move and points it at one target.
- **A reviewer.** `critique` scores the design against usability heuristics and ranks what to fix first. `audit` checks accessibility, performance, theming, and responsive behavior, with findings ranked P0 (blocking) to P3 (polish).
- **A slop detector.** 62 deterministic rules flag the tells above, plus quality problems like cramped padding and skipped headings. No LLM, no API key.

Impeccable is strongest on interfaces that already exist: point it at a page or a component and iterate. It builds new pages too; see [Build something new](https://impeccable.style/docs/new-work) for how to get the most out of that harder mode. To start, pick one component:

```
/impeccable critique the pricing cards
```

## How it works

Run `/impeccable init` once per project. It reads your code, asks only what it can't infer (who the product is for, what it needs to do, the constraints), and writes `PRODUCT.md`. Every later command reads it. Run `/impeccable document` to capture your existing visual system in `DESIGN.md`, so changes stay on-brand. [More on context files](https://impeccable.style/docs/context).

Then name a command and a target:

```
/impeccable critique the onboarding flow
/impeccable quieter the landing page
/impeccable polish settings
/impeccable harden checkout
```

Or just describe what you want: `/impeccable redo this hero section`. Narrow targets get better results; a single section reviewed closely beats a whole page at a glance. Pin a command you use often with `/impeccable pin audit` to get `/audit` as its own shortcut.

### 24 commands

| | Commands |
|---|---|
| **Steer** | `bolder` amplifies safe designs · `quieter` tones down loud ones · `distill` removes what the page doesn't need · `colorize` brings color to a gray interface · `typeset` fixes fonts, hierarchy, and sizing · `layout` fixes spacing and rhythm · `animate` adds transitions and interaction feedback · `delight` adds personality · `overdrive` goes for shaders, spring physics, and scroll-driven effects |
| **Review** | `critique` is a scored UX review · `audit` is a technical quality report |
| **Finish** | `polish` is the final pass before shipping · `harden` covers errors, i18n, overflow, and edge cases · `clarify` rewrites unclear copy · `adapt` handles screen sizes and devices · `optimize` fixes loading and rendering performance · `onboard` designs first-run flows and empty states |
| **Iterate live** | `live` lets you pick an element in the browser and cycle through variants · `generate` produces variants of a named element without manual picking |
| **Plan and set up** | `shape` plans UX before code · `init` writes `PRODUCT.md` · `document` writes `DESIGN.md` · `extract` pulls repeated patterns into your design system |

The 24th, `craft`, is a deprecated alias for a plain build request. Type `/impeccable` alone to see the list in your agent. Each command has its own page: [impeccable.style/docs](https://impeccable.style/docs).

On Codex, open `/skills` or type `$impeccable` instead of the slash command.

### Live mode

`/impeccable live` opens your running dev server with an overlay. Select an element, pick a direction, and Impeccable hot-swaps variants in place. Accept one and it is written back to your source. It works with Vite, Next, SvelteKit, Astro, Nuxt, and plain HTML. [Iterate in the browser](https://impeccable.style/tutorials/iterate-live).

Live mode edits a local checkout only; don't inject it into a deployed site or weaken a production CSP to make it work. Applying copy edits runs your `package.json`'s optional `impeccable:manual-edit-validate` script with your permissions, so review it before using live mode in an unfamiliar repo.

Apply sends staged copy edits to your chat agent while a live session is polling. If none has polled in the last minute, it runs the `codex` CLI from your PATH instead (or `claude` when codex is missing), with approvals, permission checks, and sandboxing off (`--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` or `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`) and your environment inherited. Its prompt carries the staged edits, the edited elements' HTML and nearby text, the page URL, and candidate source paths. Set `IMPECCABLE_LIVE_COPY_AGENT=chat` in the environment that starts live mode to keep Apply in your chat session, or `off` to disable Apply. The server reads it once at startup.

## Three ways to run the detector

**In your agent.** The design hook scans every UI file your agent edits and hands the findings back before the agent calls the work done. This is where most slop gets caught: without the hook, the detector only runs when someone remembers to run it. It's available on Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, and Hermes Agent, and the installer sets it up. Say yes. [Automatic design checks](https://impeccable.style/docs/hooks).

**In CI or your terminal.** The CLI needs no agent:

```bash
npx impeccable detect src/                   # scan a directory
npx impeccable detect https://example.com    # scan a rendered page (uses your installed Chrome or Edge)
npx impeccable detect --json .               # machine-readable output
npx impeccable detect --github src/          # GitHub Actions annotations
npx impeccable detect --list-rules           # every rule with its id and description
```

Source files like JSX and TSX get the pattern rules only. Rules that need a rendered page, such as low contrast and tiny text, run when you scan a URL, so point the CLI at your dev server too: `npx impeccable detect http://localhost:5173`.

Exit code `2` means findings, `1` means a target couldn't be scanned. To allow your brand font everywhere, run `npx impeccable ignores add-value overused-font Inter --reason "Brand font"`. To turn a rule off for one file, add a comment: `<!-- impeccable-disable overused-font: exported brand doc -->`. [Run a detector scan](https://impeccable.style/docs/detector) · [Configuration and ignores](https://impeccable.style/docs/config).

**In your browser.** The [Chrome extension](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/impeccable/bdkgmiklpdmaojlpflclinlofgjfpabf) overlays the same findings on any live page, yours or anyone else's. [Review with a visual overlay](https://impeccable.style/tutorials/critique-with-overlay).

## Installation

```bash
npx impeccable install
```

The installer detects your coding tools, asks whether to install for this project or globally, and offers the design hook where your tool supports one. Accept the hook. Reload your tool afterward. `npx impeccable update` refreshes an existing install. For scripts, pass `--providers=claude,codex,cursor` and `--scope=project|global`.

Three tools need one more step before the hook runs. In Codex, open `/hooks` and approve the project hook (again after an update that changes it). In Grok Build, run `/hooks-trust` or launch with `--trust`. In Hermes Agent, the hook is a plugin: run `hermes plugins enable impeccable-design-hook` once. [Allow the hook in your harness](https://impeccable.style/docs/hooks#allow-the-hook-in-your-harness).

Node is only needed for `npx`. The skill itself runs a self-contained engine binary that ships next to it or downloads once into `~/.impeccable/bin/`.

<details>
<summary><b>Claude Code, Copilot, and Grok plugins</b></summary>

**Claude Code:** `/plugin marketplace add pbakaus/impeccable`, then open `/plugin` and install Impeccable.

**GitHub Copilot in VS Code:** install [Impeccable from the Visual Studio Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=renaissance-geek.impeccable) or run `code --install-extension renaissance-geek.impeccable`. Needs VS Code 1.109.3+, Copilot Chat, and a trusted workspace. It installs the skill without the hook. [Details](docs/VSCODE-EXTENSION.md).

**Grok Build:** `grok plugin install pbakaus/impeccable#plugin --trust` installs the skill, agents, and hook.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Git submodule (a pinned version for the whole team)</b></summary>

```bash
git submodule add https://github.com/pbakaus/impeccable vendor/impeccable
npx impeccable link --source=vendor/impeccable --providers=claude,cursor
```

Commit `.gitmodules`, the submodule, and the generated links. Teammates run `git submodule update --init --recursive`. To upgrade, run `git submodule update --remote vendor/impeccable`, rerun the `link` command, and commit. Linking installs skills, not hooks. Existing skill folders stay put unless you pass `--force`.

</details>

<details>
<summary><b>Manual copy, no Node required</b></summary>

Download the ZIP for your tool from [impeccable.style](https://impeccable.style), or clone this repo: each tool's build is committed at the repo root. Copy `skills/impeccable` from the folder below into the same place in your project, or into the global folder.

| Tool | Repo folder | Global skills folder |
|---|---|---|
| Claude Code | `.claude/` | `~/.claude/skills/` |
| Cursor | `.cursor/` | |
| Codex CLI, Replit Agent | `.agents/` | `~/.agents/skills/` |
| Devin | `.devin/` | `${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/devin/skills/` |
| GitHub Copilot | `.github/` | |
| Gemini CLI | `.gemini/` | |
| Google Antigravity | `.agent/` | `~/.gemini/config/skills/` |
| OpenCode | `.opencode/` | |
| Grok Build | `.grok/` | `~/.grok/skills/` |
| Hermes Agent | `.hermes/` | `${HERMES_HOME:-$HOME/.hermes}/skills/` |
| DeepSeek Harness | `.dsh/` | `${DSH_HOME:-$HOME/.dsh}/skills/` |
| Pi | `.pi/` | |
| Qoder | `.qoder/` | `~/.qoder/skills/` |
| Rovo Dev | `.rovodev/` | `~/.rovodev/skills/` |
| Mistral Vibe | `.vibe/` | `~/.vibe/skills/` |
| Trae | `.trae/` | `~/.trae/skills/` |
| Trae China | `.trae-cn/` | `~/.trae-cn/skills/` |

For example: `mkdir -p your-project/.claude/skills && cp -r .claude/skills/impeccable your-project/.claude/skills/`.

Notes:
- A manual copy skips the design hook and subagents. Run `npx impeccable install` to get them; it writes each tool's hook pointing at the right skill path.
- OpenCode also needs `.opencode/commands/impeccable.md` copied into your project's `.opencode/commands/` to provide `/impeccable`.
- Hermes asks you to trust project-local skills once: run `hermes skills trust` from the project root. Global installs need no trust step.
- Cursor and Gemini CLI may need Agent Skills enabled in settings. See the [Cursor](https://cursor.com/docs/context/skills) and [Gemini CLI](https://geminicli.com/docs/cli/skills/) skills docs.
- Restart Trae after copying.
- `impeccable install` and `update` manage a DeepSeek Harness global copy only when `DSH_HOME` is inside your home directory.

</details>

## Project files and git

Impeccable writes its working files under `.impeccable/`. A few are shared project artifacts and belong in the repo: `config.json`, `live/config.json`, `design.json`, `surfaces/*.md`, and `critique/*.md`. Keep `PRODUCT.md` and `DESIGN.md` in the repo too. The rest is screenshots, caches, and runtime state.

<details>
<summary><b>Copy the <code>.gitignore</code> entries</b></summary>

```gitignore
# impeccable-ignore-start
# Ephemeral output, runtime state, and per-dev overrides.
# The **/ prefix covers .impeccable at the repo root or in a nested workspace.
# Shared artifacts stay tracked: config.json, live/config.json,
# design.json, surfaces/*.md, critique/*.md.
**/.impeccable/config.local.json
```

The folders that hold decision-round state (`.impeccable/questions/`, `.impeccable/mocks/worlds/`) also ignore themselves. A `.gitignore` can't untrack a file git already tracks; if you committed one earlier, run `git rm --cached <path>`.

## Good to know

**Build path.** For new landing pages and showcase surfaces, Impeccable can generate a full-fidelity comp first and build to match it (bolder, slower), or build straight in code (leaner, faster). App screens and documents are always built in code. `init` asks once and saves the answer as `buildPath` in `.impeccable/config.json`; the decision page lets you override it for one session. The choice only appears when your harness can generate images. [Image generation](https://impeccable.style/docs/image-generation) · [Configuration](https://impeccable.style/docs/config).

**Hooks run outside model approval.** In Claude Code, installed command hooks run even when you deny the model's own commands, so the first edit can download the engine. Review installed hooks before unattended runs, or pass `--settings '{"disableAllHooks": true}'` to turn them off for a run. The installer leaves hook entries it didn't add alone.

**Something broken?** `/impeccable doctor` finds stale context files, unused settings, and broken hooks. [Fix setup problems](https://impeccable.style/docs/doctor).

**Telemetry.** When a new design starts, the skill fetches a set of visual directions from the impeccable.style catalog. Turning telemetry off doesn't stop that request; it stops the anonymous record of which directions were shown and which one you picked, which is how the catalog learns what works. Your project name, files, code, and `PRODUCT.md` are never sent. Disable telemetry with `npx impeccable telemetry off`, `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`, or `"telemetry": false` in `.impeccable/config.json` for the whole project. The full list of what is sent is on the [privacy page](https://impeccable.style/privacy).

______________________________________________________________________

Monty avoids the latency, complexity and cost of a container based sandbox for running LLM generated code.
It comes in two forms: **OSS Monty**, the MIT licensed Python 3.14 sandbox you install as a package, and
[**Full Monty**](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/commercial-support/server/), the commercial server that runs the same sandbox behind a gRPC stream as a service.

A new OSS Monty sandbox takes under **1ms** from a running pool (Full Monty: about **2ms**)
[compared to](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/reference/alternatives/) around **1500ms** for a sandbox service.

Filesystem, environment variables and network do not exist inside the sandbox: it reaches the host only through the
functions and mounts you pass in.

**Documentation: [pydantic.dev/docs/monty](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/)**

## Install

```bash
uv add pydantic-monty        # Python
npm install @pydantic/monty  # JavaScript / TypeScript
cargo add monty              # Rust
```

The commercial [Full Monty](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/commercial-support/server/) runs the same workers as a container
image.

## Example

The `code` string is what a model writes when asked how long a bar of chocolate could power a lightbulb:

```python
from pydantic_monty import Monty

code = """
kcal = nutrition('chocolate bar')['kcal']
hours = kcal * 4184 / (bulb_watts * 3600)
print(f'a chocolate bar powers a {bulb_watts} W bulb for {hours:.1f} hours')
"""

with Monty() as pool:
    with pool.checkout() as session:
        session.feed_run(
            code,
            inputs={'bulb_watts': 10},
            external_lookup={'nutrition': lambda food: {'kcal': 230}},
        )
        #> a chocolate bar powers a 10 W bulb for 26.7 hours
```

`nutrition` ran on the host and the sandbox saw only its return value.

## Documentation

- [Introduction](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/) with the latency measurements
- [Comparison to alternatives](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/reference/alternatives/): Docker, Pyodide, WASI,
    sandboxing services
- Getting started with [Python](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/quickstart/python/),
    [JavaScript](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/quickstart/javascript/) or
    [Rust](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/quickstart/rust/)
- [Security model](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/concepts/security/), [resource
    limits](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/concepts/resource-limits/),
    [snapshots](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/concepts/snapshots/), [the Python
    subset](https://pydantic.dev/docs/monty/limitations/)
- [`docs/`](./docs): the source of the documentation site

Monty runs [Code Mode](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/harness/code-mode/) in [Pydantic
AI](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai).
Community bindings: [gomonty](https://github.com/ewhauser/gomonty/) (Go) and
[dart_monty](https://github.com/runyaga/dart_monty) (Dart / Flutter).
